...at the end of three years, they might then ask him any question; but by then, they had none to ask, for he had satisfied all their doubts.

And a narrow-mouthed vessel, which holds much within its capacity <note>original: in the continent</note>, you may fill with *precious liquor* and so preserve it, if you pour it in only *as fast as it can receive it*. Nor do we set young students <note>original: Schollers</note> to learn *Latin* or *Greek* at their first entrance; instead, we instill learning by degrees, as they are able to absorb <note>original: suck in</note> and receive it.

And truly, they are only (as St. John and Jeremiah say) *one from a city and two from a tribe who shall come to Zion* <note>original: "One of a City, and two of a Tribe, that shall come to Zion" — a reference to Jeremiah 3:14</note> who can attain this salvation; few there are who enter through this narrow gate. *For wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many there are who go in through it; but narrow is the gate and hard is the way that leads to life, and few there are who find it.* <note>original: "strait is the gate" — a reference to Matthew 7:13–14</note>

In reading these sermons, you may observe that the author cuts a clear path between two extremes. First, he avoids the mere *Rationalist*, who tries to measure **God** according to his own reason—otherwise, he believes he is no God at all. This group also includes the *Formalist* <note>one who focuses on outward religious rituals and rules rather than inner spiritual life</note>. Second, he avoids the *Familist* <note>a member of a mystical sect called the "Family of Love" who believed they could achieve a state of sinless perfection</note>, who claims he lives above religious laws <note>original: "Ordinances"</note> and has thus completely abandoned all religion, gradually turning into a lawless *Ranter* <note>a radical religious group often accused of "licentious" or immoral behavior because they believed they were beyond the reach of traditional morality</note>. These are the main points currently being debated, and the two great rocks upon which so many in these days have wrecked their ships (by leaning too far toward one or the other). But the author distinguishes between them so clearly that he avoids both rocks, carrying the truth forward at full speed <note>original: "Amain with Top-sail"</note> against all attacks and opposition.

# TO THE
## READER of Dr. Everard’s
# SERMONS.

*Christian Reader,*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut border composed of small floral and fleur-de-lis motifs surrounding the initial letter A.</image-desc>

As there were many causes of delay in publishing these sermons, so there are also reasons for bringing them to light now. The time when they were preached was in the days of the *last Bishops* <note>original: "last Bishops"; this refers to the high-church Anglican hierarchy under Archbishop William Laud, who suppressed non-conformist and mystical preachers prior to the English Civil War.</note>, who endeavored to *strangle* many truths in their birth—much like *Pharaoh* did to the children of *Israel*—lest they should increase and *multiply* to discover and *suppress* their deeds of darkness. To that end, they brought many precious and bright-shining lights before the *High Commission* <note>The Court of High Commission was a powerful ecclesiastical court used by the Church of England to enforce religious uniformity and prosecute dissenters.</note>, of which this author was one. They laid many foul things to their charge (as their custom was) *which they never knew* (as *David* said of himself regarding his enemies), thereby creating a great noise to distract the people for interfering with such men, and to cloak their wicked designs (for the suppression of light and *men of light*) as if these men were guilty of foul *doctrine*, or a foul *life*, or both. And though they could prove nothing against them, they still kept them in their courts, if possible, to awe and vex them, if they could not *suppress them*.

The author of this book was spotless in both his doctrine and his life, especially since God appeared to him in a special and extraordinary manner *within him* during his later days. For he confessed, along with the Apostle *Paul* in *Ephesians* 4:17, 18, that in the days of his former ignorance and vanity, he walked *as other Gentiles*, and as *men living without God in the world, in the vanity of his mind, having his understanding darkened, being alienated*

Ephesians 
4:17, 18.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the preface "To the Reader" from the previous page, detailing Dr. John Everard's trials before the ecclesiastical courts and his struggles with both the church hierarchy and his own misguided followers.</meta>

...alienated from the life of God, because of the blindness of his heart; which no doubt our merciful and ready-pardoning God had forgiven, even though men could not, or would not forget. He regarded this *not much* <note>meaning: he was not greatly concerned by the opinions of men</note>, since God spoke peace and pardon to his soul.

But afterward he desired *nothing more* than to bring in others to see what he saw, and to enjoy what he enjoyed, and to clarify the truth to them in both respects. He often declared <note>original: "averring"</note>—both to others and to the Publisher of this book—that his trouble was not because of his *own sufferings*, but because the truth might be obstructed or defamed in any way because of him.

Once he had obtained permission from their Court to refer the accusations against him—especially regarding his *doctrine* and his *conventicles* <term>secret or illegal religious meetings held outside the established Church</term> (as they called them)—he was allowed *to reason out his judgment* and explain what he had delivered with four Bishops who were *members of that court*, or any three of them. *In this* he rejoiced more than in *anything else*, as he expressed (and we judge, not without good reason). He took a great deal of pains and *effort* <note>original: "travel"; in this context, it implies arduous labor or "travail"</note> to arrange this meeting. Several times he managed to get *two* of them together, but he could never get three of them at once to confer with, or to allow him to give an account of *whatever* he had delivered. He hungered and thirsted for this meeting so that he might vindicate the Truth. We leave it to others to judge what the cause of such backwardness *in them* might have been.

But *it may be* that if they had met, they might have learned that *which they never knew*. For as *truth* is strongest, so God had wonderfully *entered into him* and declared Himself through him in his later years. God made him (as it were) a *Samson* against the *numerous* Philistines, and a *David* against the *huge* and mighty *Goliaths* of those times. For *even then*, in his days, some of his *acquaintances and followers*—who were indeed *very knowledgeable* men and claimed *High things* (as indeed they were)—abused those truths for great *licentiousness* <term>lacking moral or legal restraint; unbridled behavior</term>. They made even those precious *truths an excuse for the flesh* <note>original: "an occasion to the flesh"; using spiritual liberty as a justification for sinful or worldly behavior</note>. Consequently, he was forced to threaten to prosecute them for *punishment* because of their vile words and actions, if they persisted after he had *warned* them so often. And he forbade their...

--- Page 42 ---
<meta>This page continues the character sketch of Dr. John Everard, emphasizing his humility and accessibility to all people, regardless of their social status, and his personal transformation from a traditional scholar to a spiritually enlightened teacher.</meta>

# To the Reader.

...following or hearing him, unless they came with an affection for the truth and with a desire to be *built up in the most holy faith*. Yet, as he was a man of commanding presence and princely behavior and deportment, fit to keep company with such people, he was also familiar even with the lowliest. If they were *willing to be taught*, he was just as willing to *instruct and teach them*. Because of this, they were more welcome to him than lords or princes, as he imitated the humble conduct of his Lord and Master. He did not think it any disgrace to keep company with the worst and lowest of men, as long as he might do them good; for he knew he was not sent to call the *righteous*, but *sinners*; nor to heal the healthy, but the sick. He did not come for the *Justiciaries* <term>those who believe they are justified by their own works or legalistic righteousness</term>, and those who—though they may be *extensive* in their confession of *sin*—actually see very little of it in themselves and even less to *repent of*.

Indeed, those who were around him, whether in sickness or health, would often say they gained more *good instruction* from him in *conversation* than from many sermons by other men. He was always *eager*, even if they were *reluctant* <note>original: "backward"</note>, to find opportunities to communicate divine truths, so that he captured their attention; just as Christ did for *Mary*, who *chose that better part* which should <margin>Luke 10:42</margin> never be taken from her. 

And when they were *hesitant* to inquire of him, he would *encourage them* to ask him questions, if they had any doubts or questions to propose then. For, said he, "When I am gone, many will *miss me*; therefore I desire you to make use of me and get what you can from me while I am here. The more you do so, the more welcome you are; but I know Christ will be a teacher to those who belong to Him." 

He was also a man of an exceptional, courageous, and *discerning* spirit, endowed with the skill and depth of learning, judgment, and experience needed to *handle* what God had (though only recently) revealed to him. As he often said, *affirming* that he was *now* ashamed of his former *knowledge*, expressions, and preachings—even those from since he became a Doctor of Divinity <note>original: "Dr. in Divinity"; a high academic degree in theology</note>. Although he was known to be a *very great scholar* and as good a philosopher <note>meaning: a student of natural and moral philosophy</note> as any, with few or none exceeding him, yet when he came to *know himself* and his own heart, and also to know...

Yet, despite all this (as he said of himself), he did these things by the mere power of "self," using his natural abilities and the strength of the "old self" <term>old man</term> <note>A biblical term (Romans 6:6) referring to human nature before it is transformed by spiritual rebirth.</note> working within him. They may even suffer the loss of their wealth <note>original: "Means"</note> and liberty—or even their heads and lives—yet do so merely out of vanity or some other self-interest. In this regard, there is truly little to no difference between them and those who suffer for doing evil.

# To the Reader.

If we relate just one passage, spoken confidently by him (after God had *opened his eyes*), you might suppose there was an *extraordinary discerning spirit in him*—as if he were able—to prophesy. "My friends," he said, "remember and mark my words well: you see the Bishops now in high, great, and swelling positions, grasping all the power of both Church and State *into their hands*; but if you ever live to see a *settled Parliament in England*"—explaining his meaning this way: "I mean a Parliament having power within themselves, so that the King may not (as he has done until now) dismiss them at his pleasure—which will happen before long—you shall see the *utter downfall of the Bishops*."

This was spoken nearly *two years* before it ever happened, when there was no sign of any such thing. "Oh Sir!" replied his friend (who was present then), "how can such a thing be? They have *now* gained so much power and are so rooted by Law that such a thing would shake the very roots and foundations of the nation. Perhaps their wings may be clipped, their power weakened, and their great lordliness taken away; but for them to be *completely* removed seems impossible." "Well," he said, "despite all that, take special notice of what I say, for we *both may live to see it*: the very race and office of Bishops will be *utterly overthrown*."

Not long after, he was himself brought up again by them into their High Commission <note>The Court of High Commission was an ecclesiastical court used by the Crown to enforce religious reform and punish dissent; it was notorious for its severity and was eventually abolished by the Long Parliament.</note> and kept there waiting for a ruling until the *preparations for this downfall* began to take effect—namely, the rising of the Scots, and so on. At that point, he would say, "*The work has begun*." "And I observe," he said, "by their facial expressions, that their hearts are failing; for I see heavy lead in their eyes." His case remained pending there until he fell sick, but he lived to see *Strafford* and *Canterbury* <note>Thomas Wentworth, Earl of Strafford, and William Laud, Archbishop of Canterbury. Both were key advisors to King Charles I and were eventually executed for treason.</note> put under the Black Rod <note>To be "under the Black Rod" means to be taken into custody by the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, an officer of the House of Lords.</note>, and then *he was gathered to his fathers* <note>A biblical idiom (original: "gathered to his Fathers") meaning he died.</note>.

The author, setting himself against these errors, endeavored to *expose* <note>original: "discover"</note> them, laboring with all his *might* to uproot *unreliable* <note>original: "unsound"</note> and *literal professors* <note>Professor: someone who openly declares or "professes" their religious faith, often used here to imply those whose faith is only intellectual or surface-level.</note> from their false foundations. Yet he found that most *people* approved and commended them (though they were merely superficial), and even most ministers and preachers were *sewing pillows under their elbows* <margin>Ezekiel 13:18</margin> <note>original: "sewing pillows under the elbows"; a biblical metaphor for false prophets who make people feel comfortable and secure in their sins rather than challenging them.</note>. Therefore, lately our author seldom or never went *their way* or walked *their paths*, but intentionally avoided them. He saw that those paths led men to be, at best, only novices in Christianity, fed *always with milk* because they were unable to digest or receive *solid food* <note>original: "strong meat"</note>—their stomachs would *turn at it*. He believed people might reach that state and *yet still be nothing at all*. Therefore, his work and effort was to lay a foundation and root them firmly and steadily, *and then to build them up* and cause them to *grow up* and reach maturity <note>original: "perfection"; in this context, spiritual maturity or completion</note>. This they must do if they are truly founded upon the true cornerstone, *Jesus Christ*. 

He worked to prepare them for *solid food*, as the Apostle says in <margin>Hebrews 6:1–2</margin>: *Leaving the basic principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on to maturity, not laying again the foundation of repentance, faith, baptism, the laying on of hands, the resurrection, and eternal judgment.* Instead, as the angel commanded *John to "come up here,"* he encouraged them to look for those *full assurances* <note>original: "Plerophoria's"; from the Greek *plerophoria*, meaning complete certainty or full abundance.</note>—those rich and full things—so that we may *be in the Spirit on the Lord’s Day, as John was*. <margin>Revelation 1:10</margin> These things are offered to all who hunger and thirst for them and who cannot be satisfied without them—and to no one else.

These sermons we had much trouble keeping out of the Bishops' fingers. The author, setting himself against these errors, endeavored to *reveal* them. He labored with all his *might* to dislodge <term>original: "unbottom"; to pull someone away from their current foundation or basis of belief</term> *insincere* and *literalist believers* <term>original: "Professors"; in this period, it refers to those who "profess" or openly declare their Christian faith</term> from their false foundations. He realized people could reach that state and yet be spiritually nothing at all. Therefore, his work and endeavor was to lay a foundation and root them surely and steadily, *and then to build them up*. He aimed to cause them to *grow* and reach perfection—which they cannot help but do if truly founded upon the true cornerstone, *Jesus Christ*. 

He labored to prepare them for *solid food*, as the Apostle says in *Hebrews 6:1–2*: <margin>Hebrews 6:1, 2</margin> *“Leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance, faith, baptism, and the laying on of hands, of the resurrection, and of eternal judgment.”* Instead, he urged them as the Angel commanded *John*, *“Come up here,”* and look for those *full assurances* <note>original: "Plerophoria's"; from the Greek *plerophoria*, meaning absolute certainty or full conviction.</note>—those rich and complete things—so that we may be *in the spirit* on the Lord's day, as *John* was. <margin>Revelation 1:10</margin> These things are offered to all those who *hunger and thirst* for them and who cannot be satisfied without them—and to no one else.

# To the Reader.

Many scholars and other Christians have, from time to time—having experienced these practical spiritual matters within themselves—deemed these writings worthy of *publishing*. Although they lack much of the doctor’s <note>The "doctor" refers to the author, likely indicating he held a doctoral degree in divinity.</note> scholarship and talents <term>original: "parts"; natural intellectual abilities or skills</term>, they have now succeeded in sharing them publicly. They are confident that those who actually possess these spiritual experiences will not be critical <note>original: "captious"; prone to finding trivial faults or raising petty objections</note> or look for mistakes, *but will instead kindly accept what is well-intended*.

Moreover, another primary reason for not delaying their publication any longer is the corruption of *many truths* that have emerged more recently than in the past. Many of those "diamonds of truth" are clarified and *polished* in this book—truths that have been *greatly abused and degraded*. 

This abuse has come from two sources. First, from those "filthy dreamers" <note>A reference to Jude 1:8, a common biblical label for those who claimed spiritual revelations as an excuse for immoral behavior.</note> who have woefully mistaken, corrupted, and defiled many glorious truths. Through their false and devilish conclusions, they have not only provided an opportunity but even a justification *to indulge in physical sin* <note>original: "defile the flesh"; likely a reference to "antinomianism," the controversial belief that those under God's grace were no longer bound by moral laws</note>, falsely pretending that the Truth allows it. Of course, Truth (in itself) cannot be corrupted or defiled. 

The second source of abuse is those "blind seers" of our time. They call themselves prophets but are not; as Isaiah says in Isaiah 5:20, they "call evil good and good evil; they put darkness for light and light for darkness." <margin>Isaiah 5:20.</margin> Here, you will also find many of those diamonds and precious truths rescued from *beneath their feet*. These truths have been trampled in the dirt by those who did not know their worth, who slandered them with insulting names like "Error," "Heresy," or "Familism" <note>A radical 16th-century religious movement (the Family of Love) that emphasized internal spiritual experience over outward ceremony; it was frequently used as a slur for any mystical or non-conformist group.</note>. 

Because these critics did not recognize a *true and genuine diamond*—or if they recognized some, they did not recognize all—they immediately dismissed what they did not understand as a fraud or a counterfeit. Indeed, few people can distinguish these truths from dirt because the critics have so thoroughly smeared and trampled them in the mud. Yet in these pages, you will find them made lustrous <note>original: "orient"; a term referring to the superior luster and value of a gemstone</note>, sparkling, and radiant <note>original: "refulgent"; shining very brightly</note>, fit to be numbered among those precious foundation stones from which the New Jerusalem is built (Revelation 21). Those "blind seers" are also portrayed exactly as they are <note>original: "pourtraitured to the life"</note>, and their masks of holiness are pulled away.

# To the Reader.

...fasten your eyes on any human being <note>original: "creature"; here meaning a created being, specifically a human</note> whatever. No, no, God forbid! Let such a thought be far from us. For <margin>Isaiah 2:22</margin> what is man, or why should he be highly regarded? It was never the author’s practice to elevate "Man," nor do we present him here as a *perfect man*. Instead, like *Elijah* <note>original: "Eliah"</note>—as the Apostle says of him in <margin>James 5:17</margin>—*he was a man with a nature just like ours*.

Now, if I do what I do not want to do, it is no longer I who do it, but the *sin that lives in me*. 

He never attributed any good—whether spiritual graces or talents—to himself, but gave all the credit to God. *And he went up to the inhabitants of DEBIR; and the name of DEBIR was previously Kiriath-sepher. And Caleb said, "He who strikes Kiriath-sepher and captures it, to him I will give my daughter ACHSAH as a wife." And Othniel, the son of Kenaz and brother of Caleb, took it; and he gave him his daughter Achsah as a wife.*

He says that *Kiriath-sepher* signifies *The City of the Book*, or *The City of the Letter*. And *Debir* signifies *THE WORD*. *Caleb* means *A good heart*; *OTHNIEL* means *The Lord’s Opportunity*; and *Achsah* means *The Rending of the Veil* <note>In this mystical tradition, "rending the veil" refers to removing the barriers to spiritual understanding.</note>. So the Doctor <note>Referring to Dr. Everard</note> reads the verses in an English paraphrase like this: 

*“And ‘A Good Heart’ said, ‘He who strikes the City of the Book, or the City of the Letter, he alone shall marry Achsah and have the Rending of the Veil.’ And Othniel, ‘The Lord’s Fit Opportunity,’ he alone strikes this ‘City of the Letter’ and captures it; and to him alone the Scriptures are made DEBIR, The Word.’”* 

From this, he draws most heavenly and *divine conclusions*, and so on. But I refer you to the book itself for your further satisfaction, and I will now return to our business at hand.

The Savior says, "*You are the salt of the earth*," Matthew 5:13. Therefore, they say, He admonishes them to strive for *integrity* of life, *soundness* in doctrine, and *constancy* in suffering; for these things honor their profession, season them with *salt*, and make them savory to God and to people.

<margin>Hebrews 2:11</margin>
"*Both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all one.*" So *Jesus Christ* is the fire that salts, and the salt with which it salts, as is expressed in the verse before the text.

<margin>Matthew 5:13</margin>

# Christ the True Salt of the Earth.

When the soul becomes awakened and sees God this way—*filling all in all* and acting as the *motion* and *Agent* in all things—then it falls down before God in shame. It casts aside all its own pride and arrogance, all its high conceits <note>original: "conceits," meaning self-important ideas or notions</note> of *acting* and *doing* anything; for it sees now that it was not *the self*, but God *within* who did everything. Now, every conceit of power and spiritual gifts collapses, <margin>Ephesians 6:12, Psalm 15, Psalm 24.</margin> *along with all strongholds, all principalities and powers, and spiritual wickedness in high places.* The soul gives *all glory to God who dwells so near, in his holy hill of Zion.*

Then the soul no longer looks *outside of itself*; but <margin>Habakkuk 1:2.</margin> now it listens to know what the Lord *says within*; its eye and its ear are now turned toward Him. It will no longer rule and guide itself or take *its own advice*; rather, it sees how it has gone astray from God and desires now that God *alone* would guide it. # Christ the True Salt of the Earth.
<sig>C 4</sig>

All praise is His; and if everything belongs to Him, then what right does any creature have to claim any of it for themselves? But this great sin of arrogance is what runs through the entire world, among both the great and the small. Who even notices it? And who corrects themselves for it, asking, "*What have I done?*" This is the same spirit that rules in the *Devils* themselves; indeed, this is the *Devil* within us. For they think they possess a power of their own and so walk according to their *own* wills, not seeing that they act only by the *power* of God. God is all power and all action, and no creature stirs or moves except through Him. He is their *action* and their *being*, though He is not the source of evil. For although God is the one who orders <note>original: "orderer," meaning the one who governs or directs the outcome of events according to His purpose</note> evil, He is not its *Author*.

Yet people would use this as a reason to lay the fault on God and excuse themselves. Men have reached very strange conclusions through their mistakes: they argue that because there is in God an *active*, *positive*, *consulted*, and *deliberate* reprobation <note>original: "reprobation," the theological doctrine that some are rejected by God or predestined to damnation</note> of certain men before their sins were ever committed—even before the Creation—and because it is also said that we can do nothing without Him (*for in Him we live, move, and have our being*), they therefore conclude that the evil of an action, as well as the action itself, belongs to Him. They do not understand how to distinguish between the *Act* and the evil of the *Act*. 

No, no, you are deceived! You conclude this only because you cannot comprehend His ways, and so you try to *bound*, *limit*, and *circumscribe* the Almighty within the confines of your narrow *Reason*. But you must distinguish between the *action* and the evil of the action: *all action belongs to God*, but He is free from the evil of any *action*. All evil...

We must first have our winter and first sow our seed <margin>Psalm 126:5, 6</margin> etc., before we have our summer and time of reaping.

From this, take notice of the perpetual and constant method God uses with all His children. First, He gives them their *evening*, their *childhood* <note>original: "Non-age", referring to the period before one reaches legal adulthood</note>, and their *winter*. First, He lets them have their time of suffering, their winter of affliction, and their evening of sorrow. Their time of service comes first, and then afterward comes their *morning*, their *summer*, and their *maturity* <note>original: "Full age"</note>: their morning of joy and consolation, and their time of *reigning*. They are first servants, then heirs. 

You may observe this in those <term>types</term> <note>A "type" is a biblical person, object, or event in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic foreshadowing of Jesus Christ or Christian truths.</note> of Jesus Christ; these types represent not only His person, but also His "body" <note>Referring to the Church as the Body of Christ</note>. *Joseph* was first sold as a <margin>Genesis 37</margin> slave and was cast into prison before he was promoted to a kingdom. And *Mordecai* had his time of sorrowing and fasting before he was promoted. As Origen says, "God always begins with things that are sad, but necessary" <note>original Latin: "a tristibus semper sed necessariis inchoat Deus"</note>.

And as our Savior says in <margin>Matthew 11:28</margin> *Matthew 11:28: "Come unto me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and..."*

Beloved, these are not the sufferings the Apostle Peter speaks of in 1 Peter 4:13. <margin>1 Peter 4:13.</margin> There, he bids us *rejoice insofar as you are made partakers of the sufferings of Christ*. To suffer with and for Christ involves a different kind of suffering than these, which I shall later unfold for you. But, he says, *weep for yourselves, and for your children*: that is, for those bitter calamities that are coming upon you, the cause of which is bred within you, though you do not see it; *weep for that, lament for that*.

But secondly, some (as I said) go further than this; they suffer as Christ did *actually* <note>original: "actually" here means in physical reality or literal practice</note> with and for him, and as he commands (*as they think*) in *shame*, in *reproach*, in *imprisonment*, in *loss of goods, houses, lands, wife, and children*; yes, even in the loss of *liberty and life itself*.

But though they think it is for him, and they pretend and seem to suffer for and *with him*, yet it is not for him, but for themselves. Not only that, but many have come so far that they do not only suffer these things—enduring *poverty* and the forsaking of *houses, lands, wives, children, reputation, liberty, and life*—but they may also take pleasure in suffering with him and for him. They may indeed do this, but how do they do it? They suffer indeed willingly and cheerfully, and yet unwillingly: *Willingly*, because it may accomplish *their own ends* and *their own goals*; but they do not suffer for the sake of *his will*.

# Of suffering and reigning with Christ.

They might suffer in this way because they believe it is a path (as they think) to bring about *their own* happiness. So, even though they suffer *willingly* and might even rejoice in it, they only do so out of necessity. They see that there is no other way to heaven except through suffering and by undergoing the cross. However, *at the same time*, they *grudge* and *think poorly* of God; they *accuse* him of *severity* and *cruelty*, and think he is a *harsh master*. They also accuse the Law of severity and difficulty. They wish *the way* had been easier and smoother, without such trials and such difficult self-denial. They wish God had *pleased* them more and are ready to suggest *a better way* to him, as they think.

There is indeed a *willingness* in them to suffer and act given the circumstances, but they do not suffer *freely*; they do not *choose* for things to be the way they are. Their wills and God's will clash. *Deep down*, they do not like the cross of Christ; they wish God had done things differently rather than making their path to heaven so *rough*. They obey his commands, but they do them as a hard and painful task. These people indeed (as one writer says) *carry the cross*, but they do not *follow Christ*. Of both these types of sufferers, Christ says, "I do not know you" <note>original: *Non novi vos*</note>.

And although all these actions are like good herbs in their substance, a little bitter apple <note>original: "Colaquintida" (colocynth), a very bitter fruit known for its extreme bitterness and used as a purgative</note> among them spoils everything. Selfish motives poison it all, <margin>2 Kings 4:39.</margin> as seen in 2 *Kings* 4:39, and we may say of them, "There is death in the pot" <note>original: *Mors in olla*</note>.

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of religious efforts motivated by self-interest. It moves from warning against the "poison" of selfishness to describing a third, more spiritually mature group of believers who truly share in the life and suffering of Christ.</meta>

# Of suffering and reigning with Christ.

...poison of selfish motives <note>original: "self-ends"</note> in all you do. For you may run far, act *much*, and soar *high*; but if self is your ultimate goal, you lose *all the things you have accomplished*. Although it may seem like a *small thing* to you, it corrupts your best duties. As you know, a dead fly is but a small thing, yet it corrupts the ointment and makes it stink; so does this selfishness affect all your duties and all your actions. Therefore, I say to you, as the Apostle said to the Galatians:

<margin>Galatians 3:3, 4</margin>

Galatians 3:3, 4: *Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, will you now be made perfect by the flesh? Have you suffered so many things in vain—if it really was in vain?* 

And indeed, it is so "in vain" that there is no hope unless you recognize and correct this evil. Therefore, this must be the main thing you watch for: that this self-seeking in your actions and duties does not poison and bring all you do to nothing. For everything of this kind comes only from the *flesh* and the *self*. But *when the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and the Spirit of the Lord blows upon it, we shall see that all this is as grass, and all its goodness is but as the flower of the field*. Therefore, *arise and depart from here also; this is not your resting place.* <note>The author is quoting Isaiah 40:6-8 and Micah 2:10 to emphasize the temporary nature of human effort compared to God's glory.</note>

Following him as our *pattern*, so that in whatever condition we are in, we do the same as Christ himself would do if he were in our situation and condition.

*Objection.* But what? Are we serpents then? And do we eat the dust of the earth?

*Answer.* Yes: *This serpent* is the flesh, which first came to the woman and tempted her. I understand *Eve* to represent the *sensory* <note>original: "sensitive"</note>, fleshly, and inferior part of our nature, while *Adam* represents the rational and the *higher part* of man—namely, the reasonable soul. Now this serpent—the flesh, or this carnal part—does not first and immediately attack *Adam*, for *Adam* might have reasoned things out with him. Instead, he first attacks weak *Eve*. He first seizes the *sensory* part because it is closest to the flesh and differs very little from it. Then, at last, he gradually comes to *Adam* by way of *Eve*. In this way, the *sensory* prevailed over the *rational*, *Eve* over *Adam*, and the *woman* over the *man*.

->SERMON<-

## SERMON III.

->Romans 8:17<-

### *If so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together.*

This text, as I have told you, represents a Christian's whole life: that is, his childhood <note>original: "Non-age" — the period of legal minority or youth</note> and his adulthood <note>original: "Full-age"</note>. If that metaphor is too long, call it his winter and his summer; if that also fails, then call it his day—his evening and his morning, as in Genesis 1: "The evening and the morning were the first day." Observe: the evening always comes before the morning. 

<margin>Numbers 23:10</margin>
Now, I know everyone will be ready to say as Balaam said: "Oh, that I might die the death of the righteous, and that my last end might be like his!" (Numbers 23:10). Oh, let my adulthood be like his; let my summer and my morning be like his. The truth is, everyone would reign with Christ, but no one wants to suffer with him.

When the time comes that we must surrender these precious souls of ours, and when we feel and see that we have only our last three groaning sighs to draw <note>original: "fetch"</note>, and that we must be dissolved, departing from this earthly body <note>original: "Tabernacle" — a biblical metaphor for the mortal body as a temporary dwelling</note> and returning to the basic elements <note>original: "first principles"</note> from which we were taken, and that

<meta>catchword: that</meta>

The author observes that while many desire the rewards of the righteous, few are willing to endure the necessary suffering alongside Christ.</summary>

But this text I have now read to you withstands all these wishes and desires. In plain words: *If you suffer with Christ, then you shall be glorified with him*; if you do not suffer with him, there is no hope of glory, no hope of reigning, no hope of the crown. Therefore, it is necessary for us to look for *sufferings*. We must expect to be sufferers, and to be the kind of sufferers who may claim a part in Christ’s sufferings; for there are many sufferers in the world who yet have no part with Christ.

Furthermore, it may be that we were never whipped with Christ, never *poor* with Christ, never *crucified* with Christ, or never *imprisoned* with Christ. We were never called, as the Apostle says, *to resist even to the point of shedding blood* <note>Hebrews 12:4</note>. How, then, can we claim a share of suffering with Christ? Therefore, we must labor to find *such a condition* in which we may claim a part in Christ’s sufferings, and then we may also claim a part in his throne and glory.

For no man does evil purposely as evil, but in *his perception*, he makes it a *good* to himself before he does it, believing that he ought to do it. Yes, even *madmen*, whom we would think did evil purposely, nevertheless perceive some good in what they do.

> *If indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified together.*

If we want to know what these sufferings are that we must endure if we are to be glorified with Christ—did I say *endure*? ->1. Emptying oneself. <note>The author is referring to the concept of "kenosis" from Philippians 2:7, where Christ "emptied himself" to take on human form.</note><-
->2. Humbling oneself.<-

<margin>Romans 7:14</margin>
The Scripture then mentions three types of people who act as judges. The first are **carnal** <term>original: "carnal"; people focused on physical, worldly desires rather than spiritual matters</term> people (Romans 7:14, 1 Corinthians 3:3): *For we know the law is spiritual: but I am carnal, sold under sin. For you are still carnal: for while there is envy, strife, and divisions among you; are you not carnal, and acting like worldly men?* These people are led merely by carnal and fleshly senses, given up only to please their appetites and fleshly desires; they see no further, and their aim is no higher.

<margin>1 Corinthians 3:3</margin>
The second type are **natural or soulish men** <note>original: "Animales"; referring to the "natural man" guided by the soul/intellect rather than the Spirit</note>, whom we call **reasonable men**. These are more refined, of a higher and more sophisticated nature; they are those who mind the intellectual part—their souls. These **reasonable** or **rational men**, as we call them, are guided by reason. They stop there and are satisfied with that; for if a person can show a reason for what they do, who will condemn them? But neither of these types has the *wisdom that is from above*; for all this wisdom is *nothing but earthly, fleshly, and devilish* (James 3:15). Can it be expected that either of these two will judge themselves? Will carnal fleshly-mindedness judge carnality? No, it approves of it and justifies it. Or will reason condemn reason? How can it overthrow itself? It is impossible; *a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand* (Matthew 12:25). Yet, the rational person does judge and condemn, and often sits as judge over the actions of the carnal person.

<margin>James 3:15</margin>
<margin>Matthew 12:25</margin>
But there is a third type of people, and they are **spiritual** people (Galatians 6:1 and 1 Corinthians 2:15): *Brothers and sisters, if someone is overtaken in a fault, you who are spiritual...*

<margin>Galatians 6:1, 1 Corinthians 2:15</margin>

# Of suffering and reigning with Christ.

And I told you: no matter how much we suffer, if we do not suffer on this foundation, we do not suffer with Christ. But if we do suffer *from these two* <note>Referring to the foundations of self-emptying and humility mentioned on the previous page.</note>, then even if we suffer *very little*, we do suffer *with him*. Indeed, if these two foundations are laid, it does not matter whether we are called to suffer in the previously mentioned physical ways or not, as long as we have a readiness and a willing disposition to suffer in those ways too, if it pleases God. But by suffering in these two respects—*in emptying ourselves and humbling ourselves* as Christ did—we suffer with Christ and shall reign with him. For all other sufferings, whatever they may be, are nothing compared to these, or are nothing without these; in fact, the external and physical torments of hell are *lesser* than these spiritual sufferings. 

It may be that we are far from the physical hardships our neighbors *in Germany* <note>This likely refers to the widespread devastation and religious persecution during the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648).</note> are experiencing; yet, if we have suffered in these *two* spiritual ways, we have *suffered* more than they have, unless they have also *suffered* in these ways. All the *tyrants* in the world cannot invent tortures comparable to these internal sufferings.

Last time, we began to discuss *one* of those six steps that lead up to this *Throne of Solomon* <note>A reference to the elaborate throne described in 1 Kings 10, used here as a metaphor for the height of spiritual glory and reigning with Christ.</note>.

The first was the *condemnation of ourselves*.

The second was *self-annihilation* <term>annihilation</term>.

The third was *forsaking everything*.

The fourth was *indifference* <term>indifferency</term> to all conditions. That is, to be as willing to have pain as ease, as willing to have want as plenty, bad weather as fair, or a bad reputation as a good one—so that we can as well *bless* God for hardship as for good. Many can say, "*Blessed be his name*"

Therefore, conclude and fix this in your thoughts: if you ever swore an *oath* <note>Likely referring to a profane or false oath</note>, you are, in His sight, always swearing it. If you ever broke a covenant and promise, you are always doing so with Him. If you ever trampled the blood of the Covenant *under your feet*, you are always doing so. ### *If it is so that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together.*

Beloved, I will trust your memories for what I have previously delivered from these words, and come immediately to the second of these six steps which I have established. Consider this person in two ways:

1. Consider that whatever God gives, he claims <term>original: "arrogates." To claim or take something for oneself without justification.</term> nothing for himself and considers himself unworthy of anything. Nor can he rejoice in what he has as if it were his own, but only as a gift from God.

2. Whatever *lesson* or task God sets for this man to perform, he credits the entire power and strength for it to *God alone*. He attributes no power to himself while doing it; rather, he recognizes that he is not the one doing it, but God is working through him. Or, if he avoids any sin, he confesses that it was through no power, watchfulness, or caution of his own that he succeeded. For this is the *misery* of everyone: that a person will not admit anything except that they have *some power* of their own, believing they can do *something* by themselves. ->Rom. 8. 17.<-

### *If so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together.*

Those who have no part in Christ's sufferings have no part in his glory. These sufferings are expressed in *Philippians* 2:4 in two words:

<margin>Phil. 2:4. He emptied, he humbled himself <note>original Greek: ἐκένωσεν, ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτὸν</note></margin>
1. He emptied <note>original Greek: ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen)</note> } himself
2. He humbled <note>original Greek: ἐταπείνωσεν (etapeinōsen)</note> } himself — *Phil.* 2:7, 8.

1. In emptying himself.
2. In humbling himself.

And these are *sufferings indeed*. They are far beyond his scourgings, far beyond his being nailed to the cross, far beyond his crowning with thorns, far beyond his whipping, his mockings, and the like. All those physical sufferings *are not even worthy* to be mentioned on the same day as these. For though he was God, equal with his Father, yet he came down from Heaven *and lived among us*—among men—in the *likeness* <note>original: "similitude"</note> *of sinful flesh*, and *took upon himself the form of a servant, and made himself of no reputation* <note>This refers to the "Kenosis" or the self-emptying of Christ, where he set aside his divine status to become human</note>. And he had

Until we reach this understanding, or so far as we fall short of it, we are simply like Lucifers, mere devils. *For we are not content with God's* government, and we *dislike* <note>original: "mislike"</note> what he does; and if we had the power, we would gladly establish a government according to our own will rather than God’s. But until we come *to respect God's government as the best*, we can never *quietly* submit to it or choose it. For as long as we perceive a thing to be *evil*, we cannot help but *hate it*; it is natural for us *to hate and abhor what hurts us, and to love what does us good.*

This is why when a farmer <note>original: "husbandman"</note> experiences *bad weather* that destroys his hopes for a crop, if he perceives this *to be evil*, he cannot love the One who is the cause of it. Likewise, if a *mariner* perceives that a contrary wind is evil for him, how can he love God, who is the cause of it? In the same way, if a man thinks it is an evil to lose his father, mother, wife, children, goods, <margin>Job 2:9</margin> or lands, he cannot help but *hate Him* who is the cause of all this. As *Job’s* wife says to her husband, "*Do you still maintain your integrity? Curse God and die!*" It is as if she were saying, "*Do you still bless the God who curses you?*" This is a maxim <note>original: "maxime"; a general truth or rule of conduct</note> all too commonly accepted among us: that *where there is profit, there is piety*. We think that where God does not bless a man (according to our definition of a blessing), there can be no piety; and where He does bless a man, we think God is well *pleased*.

<summary>The author argues that true spiritual maturity requires believing that God's actions are always best, even when they cause personal loss or hardship. To resent God's providence in difficult times is compared to the rebellion of Lucifer, as it prioritizes human desire over divine will.</summary>

...and imaginations—indeed, *all the thoughts* of all the angels in heaven. For no one can comprehend God except God himself. # and the Spirit and the Life.

God is not the God of *Sunday* any more than he is the God of *Monday* or *Tuesday*, or of the *seventh* day more than any other day. Rather, he is the God of Sunday because **He is the God of Rest**. For the word [***Sabbath***] means [***Rest***]. Because all created things are in constant motion—growing, living, and acting—no creature can be at *Rest* until they return to him <note>Original: "Tim"; an OCR error for "Him."</note>; **He alone** is at *Rest*. All creatures were created by him and have (as it were) gone out from him, just as **Noah’s Dove** was sent out of the Ark. These creatures do *not rest for one minute* until they return to this **Blessed Noah** <note>The author uses Noah as a type or symbol for God/Christ, who provides the only refuge from the "waters" of worldly change.</note> again, and until **He** is pleased to reach out his hand and take them back in.

Beloved, know this: the most stable and durable creature in existence is still **in motion**; it is always and constantly **changing**. It does *not remain the same* for even **one tiny moment**. Iron, gold, silver, and stone—none are at rest, *not for one minute*. For if you could show me **any** single creature that is at *Rest* even *for one minute*, I would be so bold as to say **it was God**. That creature would be immortal and everlasting. But it is God alone who is at *Rest*; it is **He alone** who is immortal, and therefore no created thing can be. Almighty God—**He is** the True **Sabbath**. Those who return to be **one with Him** are the only ones who keep a **True Sabbath**.

<margin>Exodus 20:11.</margin>

For **God rested on the seventh day and sanctified it**. For six days **He was** creating and working. While we are absent from the Lord, we are in continual travel and labor <note>The original "travel" also implies "travail" or painful labor.</note>, and thus in continual **changing** until the "seventh day" comes. While we are in the world and in the body, we **must work** and be in a state of changing and moving from place to place, and...

They pretend to *know* so much of God’s word, as if they knew everything there is to know. ### Some Rays of Glory Appearing

This is such a truth that I would have it established and well-rooted in you: namely, that God is *He* who *fills all in all*. I would not have you ignorant of this one thing: that God is *Pure Act* <note>original: "All Act, a pure Act." This refers to the theological concept of *Actus Purus*, the idea that God is absolute perfection and activity, without any unrealized potential or need for change.</note>. Nothing acts, grows, increases, or moves except in Him. Know that *not one creature stirs in any action toward you except by divine command* <term>original: Commission</term>. There is no such thing as *chance* or *luck*. This is such a foundational truth that every branch of godliness grows from this root.

<margin>Genesis 28:16, 17.</margin>
*Jacob* saw this, for it is said: *when he awaked, then he saw God was in this place*. God appeared to him there on purpose to convince *Jacob* of this *very truth*. It was not that God was not in that place before, but *Jacob* did not see Him there before. *God was in this place before, but I did not know it*, he says. But once his eyes were opened, then he cries out, *Oh! How awesome <note>original: "dreadful." In the 17th century, "dreadful" meant "inspiring awe or profound respect" rather than "unpleasant."</note> is this place! This is none other than the house of God!* God dwells with us and in us, and yet we are not aware of it *all this while*—even to this very day.

Suppose two men were to come *into a large room* in which the King was sitting *privately* in a corner behind the tapestries. (I believe I have used this comparison <term>original: Simile</term> before, but its appropriateness makes me use it more often, so take it and apply it.) *One* of these two men spots the King, while the *other* knows nothing of him. He who knows the King is there behaves himself with all *reverence and fear* as if before the King, because he knows the King hears and sees everything. But the other man indulges <note>original: "lashes out." Here meaning to act without restraint or to burst forth.</note> in idle and shallow <term>original: frothy</term> talk, and behaves himself—

# Shadows Vanishing

*Internal essence* <note>original: "Internality"</note> and the truth of it: for the truth and substance of it do not consist either in *coldness* or in *hotness*; for it has been *hotter*, and it has been *colder*. It is neither in *old age* nor *youth*, for it has been younger and may be older. Neither is it in *heaviness* nor *lightness*, for it has been *lighter* and may be *heavier*. The truth consists in internal things, and it is the same for any other thing you *observe besides*.

And so likewise, such is the Word of God: it does not consist of anything you can *hear* or *see*, or that you can *perceive* or *comprehend*. For God’s Word is as He is—*mighty*, *incomprehensible*, *omnipotent*, etc.—and is not confined to any place. His Word is the being and life of all things. The *literal text* <note>original: "Letter"</note> cannot possibly contain the eternal majesty of the Word. It is not the *Word of God* until it is *revealed to the heart* <note>original: "expounded to the heart"</note> and made a word of power and life <term>original: "quickening"; the act of bringing to life or making spiritually alive</term> in the hearts of His people. He is happy and willing to be *something*, and to do, neglect, or know something by his own power, rather than being utterly emptied of all name, will, and work, and being subject only to God. This is the only and most deadly *sin*; indeed, it is the *sewer* <note>original: "Sink"; a place where foul liquid collects, or a drain</note> and mother of all *sin*. For the delight, will, and wisdom of the flesh is death itself; a man is no more useful, better, or religious than a pig when he dies. But insofar as he does nothing, knows nothing, and wills nothing of himself, but instead bears and endures and sees God—making a "holy day" in Him—this man keeps the Sabbath holy. Being empty of his own skill and will, he is subject only to God. In God, he goes out, works, wills, and knows—both how, what, when, and why God pleases.

Now, the whole world lies in this death and sin because it does nothing else but *kiss its own hand*—that is, it adores its own purpose, counsel, invention, and wisdom. All things are intended, aimed, drawn, and bent toward this purpose, even the Holy Scripture and the words of God: namely, they are forced to agree with our reason and not to cross our own wisdom, course, or way.

# THE
## TREE of KNOWLEDGE
### OF

### What it is.

I will not *strongly argue* <note>original: "much contend"</note> with those who insist that *the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil*, as it is recorded in *Sacred Scripture*, was a *physical tree* <note>original: "Natural Tree"</note> planted by God in *Paradise*. Nor will I argue against the belief that it was of such a *nature* that whoever ate of it would have *their eyes opened* to see their own condition, and so be made *like gods, knowing good and evil*. It may be that God intended to *admonish Adam* both *inwardly* and *outwardly* regarding what He *forbade* or *taught* him in his heart. Perhaps, *for greater clarity* <note>original: "Evidence"</note>, He likewise set this before Adam's *outward eyes*. 

But I desire, nevertheless, that they will *concede* this: that whatever was *outwardly* done also happened *inwardly* in the heart of *Adam*. There, he was *tempted* by the *seed of the serpent* to place some *value and importance* <note>original: "Account and Reckoning"</note> on his own *wisdom, will, and nature*, rather than *submitting* himself to God as one who is completely empty of his own *identity* <note>original: "Name"</note>, *knowledge*, or *achievements* <note>original: "Work"</note>. Instead, he sought to be

<summary>The author discusses the nature of the Tree of Knowledge, suggesting that while it may have been a physical tree, its primary significance was the internal temptation of Adam to rely on his own wisdom rather than God.</summary>

# The Tree of Knowledge

*something* of himself. And there are two causes that move me to think so.

The first is this: because the promise is *that the seed of the woman should bruise the head of the serpent*. Now, we read of no *physical* or *living serpent* <note>original: "Natural or Living Serpent"</note> whose head was so bruised by that seed. Therefore, I say, just as the *spiritual seed* of the woman was in *Adam's heart*, so likewise was the serpent’s seed. For man indeed was made good—not of the *substance of God*, but out of *nothing*. And therefore, he always *turns himself* from God and inclines toward *his own nothingness* <note>original: "NOTHING"</note> and vanity. For I call *the devil, sin, death, and hell, NOTHING*, as many of the ancient Church Fathers have done, and especially *Johannes Tauler* <note>original: "Taulerus"; a 14th-century German mystic known for his focus on the internal spiritual life</note>. For God never created *them*; rather, they are a *non-entity*, a *not-being*, which is contrary and perfectly opposite to *entity* and *being*. And perhaps <note>original: "Peradventure"</note> this was the *devil* that dwelt in *Adam* and seduced him, just as he did in *Lucifer*.

The other cause is this: the Scriptures likewise witness that *the City of God*, *the Heavenly Jerusalem*, and *the Kingdom of God* is a *paradise within us*. And further, that God and His Almighty Word is our paradise, *the Tree of Life, the Temple* where we dwell, *walk, sacrifice, and pray*, just as we likewise are *His temple and paradise*. And that *the Beast* spoken of in the *Book of Revelation*, which the whole world, great and small, worships in their hearts at this day—as well as *the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil*—is *within us*. For,

# Of Good and Evil.

The entire external world—and whatever either *exists* or is *done* outwardly—is nothing more than *an accident* <note>original: "An Accident"; in philosophy, a property that is not essential to the nature of a thing</note> and *a figure* symbolizing the *truth* of the thing and its *internal* nature. Therefore, nothing that is *seen* with our *eyes* is truly *real*. For the *shape* and *fashion of this world must pass away* and perish, being *nothing else* but a certain *imaginary* world—a representation of the world that is *true, right, eternal, and self-sustaining.*

Consequently, all things that were done *externally* and *symbolically* <note>original: "Signifyingly"</note> in the *Bible* must *be done again* and brought to pass *in their own way*. All the history of the Bible, all of *Moses* and the Prophets, and in short, the whole of Scripture *remains in force to this day* and is *continually* accomplished and *fulfilled internally and spiritually.* All things are *translated into the truth by Christ*. It is necessary that all the prophecies God spoke *from the beginning of the world by the mouths of His holy ones* must still be *recalled, repeated, or performed again.*

Therefore, that *shadow* or that *tree* was and is nothing else in truth but the *nature, will, knowledge, and life of Adam*. Of *this* he should not *have eaten*; *this* he should not have *ascribed* or *claimed for himself* <note>original: "Arrogated To Himself"</note>. Instead, he should have remained *free*—freely subject to God—and not have *known* anything except *what God knew* in him, nor have *done* anything except *what God did* in him, nor have *spoken* anything...

<summary>The author argues that the physical world and biblical history are merely external symbols of an internal, spiritual reality that must be continually fulfilled within the individual. He interprets the Tree of Knowledge as Adam's attempt to claim his own independent will and knowledge instead of remaining a vessel for God.</summary>

# The Tree of Knowledge

...thing, but *what God spoke* in him, and so forth in the rest.

This was so that God, *without any obstacle*, might have *exercised His almighty kingdom, will, nature, and power* within him. But Adam *himself* should have been utterly *devoid* of all *knowledge, will*, or *nature*, and should not have *claimed for himself* <note>original: "Arrogated"</note> any of these things *as his own*. This *pleased* God; this was *exactly* what He *commanded*, and what He *desired* to have *done*.

German Theology <note>original: "GERMANE DIVINITY"; likely a reference to the *Theologia Germanica*, a 14th-century mystical treatise that argues for the total surrender of the human will to God</note> agrees with this *interpretation*, concluding that this tree, in its *substance*, is *nothing else* but *our own will and knowledge*. Of these alone—in all the *earthly paradise* of the *wide world* of our hearts—*we ought not to eat*. Instead, we must account them as *forbidden*, unless we also wish to *eat of death and destruction*.

Now then, as soon as *Adam fell* and *ate of this tree*, the TREE was *immediately planted in his mind*. Afterward, it was *passed down* <note>original: "Derived"</note> into *all the branches and fruits* of his descendants. Thus, just as the *same word, precept, and forbidden status* were common to all, so is *the same fall*. All of us who are *in Adam* have now *eaten of death* and have *received* from the *serpent* this *undigested poison*. As the saying goes: *from a bad bird comes a bad egg* <note>original: "Of an ill Bird, an ill Egge"; a proverb suggesting that a corrupt source produces corrupt offspring or results</note>.

From this, it may easily be *perceived* how every man is *his own greatest enemy*, and what he *ought* to think of *himself*—of his *own will, understanding, wisdom, and knowledge*—seeing that...

# Of the Paradise of God

Just as God and the Devil are opposites, so are these two trees; they are so contrary to each other that the **one** brings life and **the other** brings death. Therefore, **it is impossible** for anyone who eats from the **one** to eat from the **other** at the same time, or even to come near it, as they are separated by a **flying cherub** and a **glittering SWORD**. I interpret these as **winged sin** and **obstinate disobedience**, which is called elsewhere in Scripture **a separation**. For whoever **eats** from the **Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil**—that is, whoever **greedily swallows down** and **devours human and diabolical wisdom**—is already separated from the **Tree of Life**; that is, from the **wisdom, speech, and knowledge of God**.

Neither of these **wisdoms, speeches, wills**, or **knowledges** can endure the **other**, nor can anyone pass from one to the other. So great is the **gulf** between them, being as far divided as heaven and hell. He who **eats** of the **Tree of Life**—that is, **of the Word of God**—is born of God and cannot die, nor even sin. For **their fruit eats the eater** <note>This mystical concept suggests that rather than the person merely consuming the fruit, the divine nature of the fruit consumes and transforms the person into itself.</note> and translates <note>original: "Translate"; to move or change from one state to another, especially from the physical to the spiritual.</note> him into **his own nature**, which is **life**. As the Scripture says elsewhere regarding the **eating of Christ’s flesh**; for indeed, it is the same thing to eat Christ, to live in His Word, to believe, to know God, and the like.

Likewise, it is **the same thing** to be in **Adam**, to live in **Adam**, to die, to eat of the **Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil**, to obey the seed and word of the serpent, and to become **GODS** <note>This refers to the serpent's promise in Genesis 3:5 that "you shall be as gods, knowing good and evil," which the author views as a state of prideful separation from God.</note>.

# The Tree of Life, etc.

**Adam** and the **wisdom** of the **flesh** must **die in us**, so that **Christ** may **live in us** and **the Spirit** may have the **government** <note>original: "Government"; here meaning the rule, authority, or sovereign control over a person's life.</note>. **The life** of the **one** is always **the death** of the **other**, and **the weakness** of the **one** is **the strength** of the **other**.

# Concerning that Great Idol of Human Wisdom and Knowledge; How men kiss their own hands, and how the whole world diligently worships only ITSELF and the works of its own hands—that is, the inventions, arts, and plans of their own reason and wisdom.

What else is the worship of idols, superstition, witchcraft, evil doctrine, and the laws <note>original: "Ordinances"</note> of men, but the *wisdom, reason, inventions, crafts, actions, instincts,* and *prudence* of humanity? Therefore, worshipping idols is merely the act of fashioning a *form* resembling God, which is not based on His word—as He teaches, figures, and forms Himself within us—but is instead based on our own opinions and judgment of God. 

Moreover, what is sin other than our own *will, wisdom,* and *counsel*, which was sown in the mind of *Adam* and his descendants <note>original: "posterity"</note> by the seed of the serpent? In this state, every person wants to be their own God: to lead, teach, govern, motivate <note>original: "Actuate"</note>, avenge, defend, excuse, and enrich themselves. Yet the sin and fall of *Adam* is nothing but human obsession <note>original: "Affectation"</note> with the cunning, reason, and wisdom of the flesh. ### SERMON I.

As this Psalm was undoubtedly *David’s*, it is more than probable that the occasion for writing it (as you may see at the beginning of it) was the moving of the Ark to *Jerusalem*, the City of *David*, from the house of *Abinadab* (2 *Samuel* 6). At that time, *David* <margin>2 *Samuel* 6</margin> with the rest of the people of *Israel* played all kinds of instruments and danced before the Ark <note>The Ark of the Covenant: a sacred chest containing the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments, representing the presence of God.</note>. Because of this, *Michal* his wife, *Saul’s* daughter, looked down on him as a fool. A rush of joy seized his spirit; because he experienced so much of God’s presence in that moment, it caused him to leap and dance before the Ark. She then took it upon herself to reprimand, judge, and insult him, and in her heart she scorned him, as the text says in verse 16. But *David*, being uplifted and <margin>Verse 16.</margin> filled with divine joy, ignored her and told her that he would become even more humble <note>original: "vile"; David means he is willing to appear even more undignified in the eyes of the worldly to honor God.</note>.

The reason for this conclusion is that this Psalm begins with that very proverb that was commanded to be said whenever the Ark was moved from its place: *Numbers* 10:35. <margin>Numbers 10:25 <note>The original text cites Numbers 10:25, but the prayer "Arise O Lord..." is found in Numbers 10:35.</note></margin> *"Arise, O Lord, and let your enemies be scattered; let those who hate him flee before him."*

I do not dare to propose any formal method for the whole text, nor any strict connection between its parts. I find that all your overly precise <term>dichotomizers</term> <note>Those who insist on dividing every text into two opposing parts or rigid logical categories, a common practice in 17th-century academic preaching.</note> do nothing but dream and play with the Scripture, feeding themselves with fancies...

If you frown at it, it will frown at you; if you laugh at it, it will laugh at you; if you hug it, it will hug you; if you strike it, it will strike you; if you embrace it, it will embrace you; if you turn your back on it, it will turn its back on you.

Just so it is with our righteous God; as a person behaves toward him, so he will show himself toward them: *If we forsake him, he will forsake us*, 2 Chronicles 15:2. If we are stubborn toward him, he will be *stubborn* toward us. But if we cling to him, he will cling to us; if we embrace him, he will *hold* and embrace us; if we run toward him, he will run toward us. Consider what the father of the Prodigal Son <note>original: "Prodigals father"</note> did; when the son was *still a long way off*, but *coming* and returning to his father, his father *ran to meet him, fell on his neck, and kissed him*. # *Militia Caelestis* <note>original: "Militia Cœlestis," Latin for "The Heavenly Host" or "The Heavenly Warfare"</note>, or

into them all, as the River Thames or the sea flows into all the adjoining *creeks* and *arms* through its streams. It fills every one according to their own capacity; it does not fill them according to its own *greatness*, but according to the greatness or smallness of those *creeks*. In this same way does our infinite God flow into all his creatures. (Yet these expressions are infinitely below him and are too narrow to fully describe God to you, but they serve as a form of resemblance.) I say that in this manner the Almighty flows into all his creatures: into angels, *archangels*, *cherubim*, and *seraphim* <note>original: "Cherubims & Seraphims." In Hebrew, the "-im" ending is already plural, but 17th-century authors often added an "s" as well.</note>; into *men*, *beasts*, *birds*, and *fish*; and into all creatures. Yet he does so not according to his own *infinite* greatness, but according to what every one can *receive* of him, and according to their individual capacity.

<margin>Exodus 33:20</margin>
For if God should *fill* his creatures or communicate himself to them beyond their capacities, he would destroy his creatures. As for *Moses*, *God showed him as much as a creature could see and live*. For if God had showed him *more*, he would have been blinded and undone by it. Things may be just as *invisible* by *too much* light as by *too little*—by an excess of light as much as by a want of light. Consider the sun: if it should shine upon us with that excess of light that is *in itself*, and if it were not intercepted and interrupted by vapors and by thick, dull air—or if we were nearer to it than we are—we should see *nothing* at all. ### The Heavenly Host

Christ lives in every person in terms of his own nature, and he is as *much* in one person as he is in another. But I say that this is the only difference: to the one, Christ is *manifested*, but to the *other* he is not. God lives in everyone, but *not everyone knows it*. A *good person has God within them*, and they *see, know, and believe it*. Others neither see, know, nor believe it, and so they do not rejoice in the *manifestations* of God within them. Instead, they believe they have a *power, will*, and a *being* of *their own*. They *glory* and *rejoice* in this, <margin>Habakkuk 1:16; Acts 17:28</margin> *presuming* upon it and living for *themselves*. They *sacrifice to their own nets* <note>original: "drags"; a reference to Habakkuk 1:16, meaning they credit their own tools and efforts for their success</note> and do not regard *God, in whom they live, move, and have their being*.

Again, would you see God in the *Sun, Moon*, and *Stars*, or in *beasts* or *trees*, and in all other creatures? Know that he is the *Life, Action, and Motion* of *all creatures*. If you take away from any or all of these everything that can be removed—all *accidents* <term>In traditional philosophy, "accidents" are the non-essential qualities of a thing (like color, shape, or size) that can change without changing the thing's basic nature</term>—then what remains is *God*. 

In the *Sun*, the *Moon*, or anything else, you must first strip it of all *visibility* and of *all form* and *representation*, whether *glorious* or *lowly*. Then you shall behold God, *not as that specific form*, but as the *Cause, Essence*, and *Being* of whatever is in it. Or, as in a human being: take from them *high status* and *low status* (for those are *accidents*), *weight* and *lightness, greatness* and *smallness, youth* and *age* (for all these are *accidents*). What remains then but he who *was, and is, and is to come*—the *All in all*? He who is *Alpha* <margin>Colossians 3:11; Revelation 1:8</margin>, the *first* of all, and shall be *Omega*, the *last* of all. What remains then but the *firstborn of the Father, Jesus Christ*? Even him who is the *Ancient*...

# The Heavenly Host, or

<margin>Numbers 10:36</margin>
*Here a specific number is used to represent an unknown or vast amount, as is often done in Scripture. For example, in Numbers 10:36, when the Ark was set down to rest, this proverb was appointed to be spoken: "Return, O Lord, unto the many thousands of Israel." In that passage, an indefinite number is used; however, as noted in the margin, the word can signify either a specific or an indefinite number—it can mean either. This interpretation led Jerome <note>original: "Hierome"; St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note> and Novatian <note>original: "Novatianus"; an early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 200–258 AD).</note> to state clearly that there are "twenty thousand," or "thousands" of angels—meaning they are innumerable, infinite, and immense. I believe this interpretation is the most accurate and consistent with biblical phrasing and the meaning of the word used here and elsewhere. For instance, the Hebrew word **Ribboth** signifies "ten thousand" in all contexts, and **Ribbaboth** is interpreted in 2 Samuel 18:7 as "ten thousand." Furthermore, **Rebaboth**, the plural form, is translated in Numbers 10:36 as "the many thousands of Israel." These words all derive from the verb **Rabbah**, meaning "he multiplied" <note>original: "multiplicavit"</note>, and **Rab**, meaning "many" <note>original: "multus"</note>. These linguistic roots gave Jerome and Novatian the insight mentioned previously.*

Therefore, the chariots of God are numberless; that is, no human can count them. This does not mean that God cannot count *them*, for He calls them all by their <margin>Psalm 147:4</margin> names, just as *David* says of the stars in *Psalm 147:4*. Any number that can be counted by humans is merely like the "number of the beast" in *Revelation 13:18*, which is described as the *number of a man*. However, *God numbers all things; for since He made all things*

There is much debate <note>original: "adoo"</note> about this name *Angels*—what they are and what their nature is—but we will not dwell too much on that now. Most people agree that all created things are *Angels*.

The word itself signifies, especially in this place, an *ambassador* or a *messenger*. Since all creatures are messengers or ambassadors from God, they must all be *Angels*. But some may further object to me, and it is a strong objection.

<margin>Objection</margin>
**Objection:** Since God is so constant and so unchangeable as he is, and he is present within his creatures, what is the reason then that the creatures are so changeable? Scripture tells us God is immutable <note>original: "Immutable"; unchanging over time or unable to be changed.</note>.

<margin>Answer</margin>
**Answer:** Beloved, Almighty God is like the sun riding in its chariot (we have no better way to describe these inexpressible things to you). The sun shines on us, yet it appears much changed to us depending on the different objects it shines through. The sun is not the same to us as it is *in itself*; for it is exceedingly bright and exceedingly hot, and its shining through the thick air changes how it appears to us, though nothing has changed in the sun itself. So, though the creature may be changed, *God is not changed*; rather, his works are changed according to the various subjects he works upon.

Again, the same beam that shines in at one window is not the same as the one that shines in at another. Yet we say the sun shines in both, even though it alters within a very small distance: in one pane <note>original: "quarrel"; a small, usually diamond-shaped, pane of glass.</note> it shines red, in the next green, and so on. Now, here is a change, but the sun is the same. So, though creatures may be changed and turned upside down, and mountains be hurled here and there, yet *God is the same*; he is not changed, and he cannot be moved. <margin>James 1:17</margin> *In him is no variableness nor shadow of changing* (James 1:17), although according to the various creatures he works in,

*Application 3.* And lastly, learn from this that there is no such thing as *Fortune*, but everything happens and turns out by an infinitely wise *Providence*. The name "Fortune" is a useless <note>original: "Idle"</note>, heathenish, and wicked word, based on what the word *implies*; for nothing happens by *Chance* or *Fortune*, but it is God who guides everything.

And yet, if we know the right use of that word, it may be *used*, for it is used in the Scriptures. *Solomon* says: *For Time and chance—or fortune (for they are the same)—happens to all things.*

Although this concept first arose from a bad foundation and from the Heathens, it was because there were *such contradictory events* in the world. When a business was brought to its conclusion <note>original: "head and period"</note>, one thing or another often came between *the cup and the lip* (as we say) and completely turned everything around. They were so amazed and at their wits' end that they could not understand how this could happen, unless there was a God called [Fortune], and therefore they sacrificed to him. But I say that if the original *foundation* and *misuse* are forgotten, it may in time become lawful to use the word, at least by those who know...

among women. She cannot be so eager in requesting anything from him as he is ready to help her. If she desires to have her name written in the palms of his hands, he will do
<margin>Song of Solomon 8:6</margin>
more: he will set her as a *seal <note>original: "Signet"; a small seal used to authorize documents, symbolizing a precious and inseparable possession.</note> upon his heart*, as you may perceive in reading through this *Book*. This *Lord* spoken of here is such a *Lord* whose judgment you cannot reject once you know him; for he is *Christ Jesus, the Lord of life and death*. And this *Lady* is the *Spouse* of this *Lord*—namely, the *Congregation* <note>original: "Congregation"; here referring to the collective body of believers or the Church.</note>, or the body of his *Saints* and *Servants*. Do not wonder that I call her a *fair Lady*; for though we may not see it, yet *He*, her *Lord*, says *she is all fair, and there is no spot in her*:
<margin>Song of Solomon 4:7</margin>
And I tell you, if we want to see the beauty of the *Church*, we must not look at any one particular member. If we do, we can never say *she is all fair*; you shall see many *spots* and many *wrinkles* in them. But if you look upon the whole *Church*, then she is *all Fair*—that is, the *complete* body together. Just as with any *species*, its *excellence* cannot be known by any one *individual*. The literal text <note>original: "The Letter"</note> is only a lifeless image or picture of the life within; it represents both the good things promised and the evils threatened. # The General Spread of Covetousness
