### The Universality of Greed

Indeed friends, it is a very hard thing to expose <note>original: "uncase," meaning to strip away a disguise</note> this sin, because one may and must have care and diligence. This is its **cloak**; **DILIGENCE** is the cloak of greed <note>original: "Covetousness his Cloak"</note>, never off its back, by which it is sheltered against all reproof.

<margin>Proverbs 30:8,9</margin>
I suppose, and it is certain, that a person may pray Agur's prayer without being greedy <note>original: "without Covetousness"</note>, Proverbs 30:8-9: *Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is right for me.* A sufficiency <note>original: "competency"</note> of food and clothing <note>original: "raiment"</note> is certainly the limit and boundary of our desires. But then another question will arise:

->*What is a sufficiency? or what is enough?*<-

Therefore, some in response to this have defined greed <note>original: "Covetousness"</note> to be an excessive <note>original: "inordinate"</note> desire for more, and the use of unlawful means and ways to get it. But I believe this is defined somewhat too favorably; for one may be greedy—even *deeply* greedy—and yet obtain their goods without fraud, deceit, or oppression, etc. As Saint Augustine wrote in *On Free Choice of the Will*, Book 3, Chapter 17: Greed is wanting more than is enough <note>original: *Avaritia est plus velle quam satis sit*</note>. It is greed to desire more than is sufficient, which is only "daily bread"; and only, "Give us *this day* our daily bread"; we have no authorization <note>original: "warrant"</note> to seek more.

But since we have daily bread—according to what our Savior teaches us to pray in the Lord's Prayer, which includes all things necessary for this life, such as food and clothing—without question, this is **sufficient**, and the desire for more is greed. As our Savior commands,

<summary>The author explains how greed hides behind the guise of "diligence" and defines it as desiring more than the "daily bread" or basic necessities mentioned in Agur's prayer and the Lord's Prayer.</summary>

To what end, then, is all this worrying? <margin>Luke 12:20</margin> For then, *you fool, whose shall those things be which you have provided?* We ought to keep ourselves within this boundary; for no sooner are we over this fence and the limit of what is SUFFICIENT, but we are in the wide wilderness and the boundless <term>CHAMPAIGN</term> <note>original: "champaign" refers to an open, flat field or broad stretch of countryside</note> of greed <note>original: "Covetousness"</note>, which consists of two things:

1. To be greedy is to let our desires run out to seek eagerly after more than what is *sufficient* for the preservation of nature in its own kind, and to not remain neutral <note>original: "indifferently affected"</note> in the use of lawful means, whether God chooses to give more or less.

2. An excessive <note>original: "inordinate"</note> love for what a person already has, even if he does not have more than what is sufficient, is greed. In this sense, a poor man may also be greedy.

<summary>The author defines the limits of material desire based on the biblical concept of "daily bread," arguing that greed begins when one seeks more than what is necessary or becomes excessively attached to what they already own.</summary>

# The General Prevalence of Greed

Greed <note>original: "Covetousness"</note> may be either in—

*   **Scraping** <note>original: "Scraping" refers to the aggressive acquisition of wealth</note> → **Rapacity** → A large paw to grasp fast.
*   *or*
*   **Holding** → **Tenacity** <note>original: "Tenacity" here means an obsessive refusal to let go of money</note> → In a clenched <note>original: "shrunk"</note> hand to hold.

In sum, I believe greed is an excessive <note>original: "inordinate"</note> desire and effort to obtain these outward things beyond the limits of what is sufficient for the preservation of one’s life and status, as I previously stated.

Beloved, this sin is like poison: it destroys and kills unnoticed and unseen. It infects the blood by degrees, whereas some other sins break out more openly and suddenly in blotches, boils, and plague-sores.

But we may observe the footsteps and show you some symptoms of this greedy man, by which he may be discovered and detected—primarily to himself, so that he may confess his guilt. For example:

1.  **In his course of life, behavior, and actions.** His time, his life, and his actions are wholly consumed in buying and selling, in commercial business <note>original: "trafficking"</note>, trading, and figuring out how to grow rich and get more. All his thoughts, words, and all his strength and efforts run in this channel. Here, greedy people are in their own element, like a fish in the water. Here their hearts run out freely, and they never regard their immortal souls. They are just like the people of the ancient world <note>original: "old world," referring to the world before the Great Flood in the time of Noah</note>:

<margin>Luke 17:26, 27</margin>
*Luke 17:26, 27: They ate, they drank, they married, and they were given in marriage...*

<summary>The author defines greed as an "inordinate desire" beyond sufficiency and categorizes it into two forms: rapacity (aggressive getting) and tenacity (stingy holding). He compares greed to an invisible poison and notes that a key symptom is a life entirely consumed by trade and material gain to the neglect of the soul.</summary>

But because this sin is so *common*—and indeed *widespread* <note>original: "Epidemical"</note>, as I have shown you—and because it is a *root* itself from which so many evil branches spring and grow, I thought it good to spend this short time (though it is not my usual way of speaking to you) if it might please God to bring anyone here to abandon and detest this great and mighty sin of greed <note>original: "Covetousness"</note>.

Some sins are specific to the position of kings. Because they have acquired so much power, they want to be *monarchs* without restraint. Their claim is *that they are accountable for their actions to no one but God alone*; and they do not lack *flatterers* and *sycophants* to preach such *teachings* in their ears—claims *that no power on earth should hold them accountable* because they *are above the law*. Then greed will cause them to make their *lusts* their *law*, and they will *take* whatever they want, whether it is right or wrong. But in this nation, they have always been restrained and kept from this *absolute power* by one means or another.

By doing so, they seized not only his vineyard but his entire estate. Greed will cause even kings to do this, and anything else, if they only have enough power.

# The Prevalence of Covetousness

What have you gained by all your care and toil, even if you had gained the *whole world*?

Beloved, God so hates this sin and this sinner, that in one prophecy he has sworn two oaths against it.

Thus, I have endeavored to *expose* <note>original: "uncase"; to strip away a mask or covering to reveal the true nature of something</note> this loathsome, unprofitable, and burdensome sin of covetousness; and if the Lord has been doing that *in your hearts* which I have been doing *to your ears*, this will be a happy meeting.

# The Further Beyond <note>original: *Plus Ultra*</note> of the Creatures.

duty: he does his duty like a *faithful* preacher, whether those he preaches to choose to hear or not; he will still discharge his own soul. A true preacher speaks the truth and calls upon them to *hear*, even if his listeners <note>original: "Auditors"</note> sleep and pay no attention to it. So likewise does *David* in this sense with these creatures; he does his duty and calls upon them to do it, even though they do not *understand* or *comprehend* it.

<margin>Reason 2</margin>
The second reason may be this: he does it craftily, as a matter of policy, to incite others to perform this duty. If *such creatures as these* ought to do *this*, then those who are above them *in rank* <note>original: "degree"</note> have even more cause to do so, and should be ashamed to neglect it. Just as an ill-behaved <note>original: "ill-governed"</note> master might stay home himself but still sends *his servants to church*, so *David*, being *conscious* of his own *neglect*, calls upon others not to be *slack* and *negligent*. Although he fell infinitely short of what he should have done, he still shows his own desire to perform this duty.

<margin>Reason 3</margin>
But if these reasons do not satisfy *you*, though they have satisfied *others*, a third reason may be this: to set forth the sweet harmony that exists among all God’s creatures. *To show* how all creatures, being God's family, speak and preach God’s praise aloud with *one consent*. Therefore, he calls upon *some* above him, some below him, and some on both sides of him—*everywhere*—to speak God’s praise. For every creature, in its own place, status, and calling, shows forth their Creator’s praise, even if in a *mute <note>original: "dumb"</note> sense and way*.

# The Further Beyond <note>original: *Plus Ultra*</note> of the Creatures.

<margin>Reason 4</margin> Or fourthly and lastly, which I think to be a good reason: **zeal makes men speak and utter things that are impossible.** The fire of zeal will so transport a man that it will make him speak of things that are **unreasonable or impossible.** For example, *Moses* in his zeal desired God, for the safety of *Israel*, to blot his name out of His book; and *Paul* wished himself <margin>Romans 9:3</margin> **accursed or separate from Christ** <note>original: *Anathema Maranatha*; from Greek and Aramaic, meaning "accursed" and "the Lord has come"</note> for the sake of his brothers' salvation. This was an impossible thing; it could not happen. But I think *David* does not intend that here, for he calls for **nothing** but what is already being done, and which is therefore possible. For **no creature can turn out of the way of His praise.** For God is not only glorified in their graces, but just as much in their sins and rebellions against Him. Even if men should spit their malice and their blasphemies in the very face of God their Maker, yet they **do not hurt Him**. They cannot touch Him nor His sacred glory. His praise shall arise entirely as much from their **destruction** <note>original: "confusion"; often meaning a state of being utterly ruined or put to shame</note> as from their **salvation**. The hurt is their own, not His.

And now, to show you how the dumb and deaf **creatures** sing praise to God, as God demanded of *Job* when **he thought as we do**—that <margin>Job 38:7</margin> only man praises God. In Job 38:7, God says, "**Where were you when the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?**" God says there that they **shouted and sang**. Did you not hear them? Did they not sing and shout in your ears? It does not matter; they did so in His.

Even these unreasoning creatures have a religion in their own way, according to God's will. We see they will acknowledge their owner, and there is obedience even in the seas. Indeed, every creature does its duty—except for **MAN**.

We will now also see if we can discover their religion. Religion consists of four parts; all religion, I say, may be reduced to four main headings:
1. A **creed**: what we are to believe.
2. A **petition**: what we are to pray for.
3. A **decalogue** <note>The Ten Commandments; here referring to a moral code of conduct</note>: what we are to do.
4. And lastly, a **sacrifice**: what we are to give.

Now let us see how all these are applicable <note>original: "competible"</note> to all these creatures. First, regarding their **creed**—what they believe and what faith they have. It is true they cannot speak as we do, yet they speak in their own way, as they are able. We require no more of children than they are able to give, and neither does God expect more of His creatures. And so these creatures, in their own way, both speak and believe.

### The Further Beyond <note>original: *Plus Ultra*; Latin for "further beyond" or "more beyond"</note> of the Creatures.

This is an undeniable maxim <note>original: *maxime*; a fundamental principle or rule of truth</note>: that there is a God. For who can look upon an *effect* without necessarily turning to *the cause*? There can be no *effect* without a cause. If we see a thing made, we know it has a Maker; and if we look upon a creature <note>In this context, "creature" refers to any created thing in the universe, including inanimate objects and animals</note> in this way, as *an effect*, it plainly points to a cause. Thus, we can look at no creature without inquiring after God. There is no attribute ascribed to God that all the creatures do not *speak of and confess*.

First (to speak of some of His attributes), for instance, God is one *simple essence* <note>In traditional theology, "simple" means not made of parts; God is indivisible and purely Himself</note>. This unity is testified and declared by the creatures: that *God is one*, and can be no more. For if there were more than one Creator of them, then the one would destroy, confuse, and overthrow the other. If there were two, they must be either *equal or not equal*. If they are *not equal*, then one is greater than the other, and the greater will overcome the lesser. If they are *equal*, then there must be bounds and limits set for how far the *one's* dominion must reach, and how far *the other's*. But to affirm this is most absurd and ridiculous.

Secondly, they all testify that *God is good*. And if He is *good*—and the only goodness, goodness itself—then likewise He must be Truth, *Entity, and Being* <note>original: *Entity*; the state of existing</note>; for all these are one. Whatever is one *is God*; whatever is truth *is God*; whatever is good *is God*; whatever is *Entity and Being is God*. For in saying He is good, or in saying He is any of these, He is all of these:

Therefore, when we behold and see the **sun**, **moon**, and **stars**, and the glorious **firmament**, we cannot help but ask, "Whose light is this?" But in us there is **such a great deal of ignorance** (which I was about to say was the **greatest sin**) that we are so far from using them as we should—**making them serviceable to us** and keeping them in their place—that we are instead **serviceable to them**. We are their servants, and we make them **masters**. We are sooner turned **into their nature** <note>original: *kind*</note> than they are into ours.

# Of Meat for Strong Men.

It is a dangerous thing (especially in recent years) to press God with specific requests for **temporal things** <note>worldly or physical concerns</note>, such as **health**, **wealth**, **honor**, and so on. Instead, we should leave all those things to the **will of God**, walking forward in our duties and calling, and leaving the **success** to Him. 

But while we are in our **childish** condition, we are constantly telling **God** what He should do for us in this regard, and how He should govern the world: when we would have **fair weather**, when **rain**, and when a **fair wind**. In this way, every person seeks to serve their own interests. And then, I ask you: if your will is done, who shall take care of your neighbor? It seems not to matter to you if thousands suffer <note>original: "miscarry"</note> and fail to receive those things, so long as you have them. 

What kind of prayers (do you think) are these? Do you truly believe that **God** would be wise if He were to answer your prayers? That which is for your benefit (as you imagine) is against the interests of many others, and who shall look out for their good? That wind that serves your purpose is just as much an opposing wind for others. 

Therefore, my advice is: be very careful <note>original: "tender"</note> how you pressure the infinite wisdom of the **Almighty**. When He intends to bless, He will turn "crosses" <note>burdens or trials</note> and evil things (as you judge them) into the greatest blessings. Therefore, let the **Almighty alone** in governing the **heavens** and the **earth** by His power and wisdom. He has upheld, supported, preserved, and ordered the **heavens** and the **earth**—to our knowledge—well enough for almost six thousand years, and I guarantee you He will continue to do it **without your worry or direction**. Well, we do not need to provide any further examples. What might the Holy Spirit's meaning be in all of this? In one word, I will tell you what a shepherd is: a shepherd is one who lives purely and most appropriately by the *providence* and blessing of God upon his *occupation* <note>original: "Trade"</note>. For they grow and increase only by God's will, blessing, and providence. He does not act much on his own, but resigns his will and all he has to God alone, depending entirely on Him. But a *farmer* <term>husbandman</term> is one who, while expecting God's blessing, joins to it his own efforts: plowing, sowing, reaping, rotating his ground, rising early, and going to bed late.

Well, I ask, is there any harm in all this? No, I do not forbid them from doing these things. But I say this: *a shepherd's life is preferred by God far more than a farmer’s, because he who has given up everything to God—all that he can ever do, say, or think—* has surrendered his entire being <note>original: "his whole man"</note> to God. Such people confess that they are *nothing* and can do *nothing*. From their very souls, they acknowledge (and not just in words) that they have *no wit, no reason, no will, and no understanding* of their own. Their whole being, all that they are or can do, is completely *resigned to God and His will*. Nor will they join any of their own works with God's, but instead let God *act all, do all, think all, and speak all* within them.

This is the life of a true shepherd, who keeps his eye *focused solely on God* <note>original: "single, on God"</note> and looks to Him in everything.

*God* is the **substance** of all things, but all things that are visible are but **shadows**, mere appearances and **bubbles**—soon rising and soon bursting, like bubbles in the water.

The reason why we are so disturbed <note>original: "disquieted"</note> by the loss of them is because we mistake the *shadow* for the *substance*. If that shadow vanishes, we must naturally be disturbed, and we are thrown completely out of order. Then, even if **God** gives us whatever **He** desires, nothing will please us. Why? Because *our Absalom is dead* <margin>2 Samuel 18, last verse</margin> <note>2 Samuel 18:33. For the world's love and joy bring only grief and sorrow in the end. But these people may rejoice that they ever had such a joy, and such a person loves **God** for giving him that love.

Until we have forsaken everything, **God** will never appear to us. # The Mystery, or Life, and

...fumes <note>original: "fumes," referring to the vapors or steam from the distillation process mentioned on the previous page</note> *nothing*; for, where should they go? They cannot go out of the world, and they cannot be turned into nothing except by God himself. For *all creatures cannot reduce the smallest gnat to nothing; this is an undeniable maxim: the same power is required to annihilate something as was required to create it.* All the kings on the earth cannot reduce *one* creature to nothing. If they should *burn* this body of mine to ashes and scatter the ashes in the air, or cast them into the river, yet there is nothing lost of me; instead, every element simply takes its part, *to which it returns.* <note>The author argues for a form of "conservation of matter," suggesting that while form changes, the underlying substance created by God is never destroyed.</note>

Now I say, Christ Jesus is this FIRE. It is 
<margin>Job 38:14</margin> he who *burns the bush, but does not consume it.* It is he (as *Job* says) who *turns them like wax to the seal.* You know that wax is *altered* and changed into *any form*; and however often you change it, *the seal*—the *form* you last gave it—*remains* until you destroy it and give it another. So does Jesus Christ: out of one and the same elements, he daily makes, unmakes, and remakes *new forms and new impressions.* And whatever impression it last had *remains* until he causes it to return, until he unmakes it and makes it anew again. And I dare to boldly affirm that if our great and glorious God should weigh the heavens and the earth now, just as he did at their creation—for the Scripture says, *He measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and contained the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales and the hills* <note>A reference to Isaiah 40:12</note>—

# True and Divine Exorcism, or

Some sins are like the sons of Anak <note>original: "Anack"; a race of giants mentioned in the Bible (Numbers 13:33)</note> in their stature and growth: mighty, great, and strong. Others are of a smaller and lower size. There are also differences in the length and duration of sins; as Job says, *His bones were full of the sins of his youth* <note>Job 20:11</note>. Some people do not leave their sins but instead increase them, carrying them within themselves until they die, and those sins grow strong and numerous, even into a Legion <note>A term for a large unit of the Roman army, used in the New Testament to describe a multitude of demons</note> of devils. <margin>Jonah 4:7.</margin>

Instead, he stays inside all the more and strengthens his possession.** This is like the natural changes in our bodies, which cannot be seen as they happen: infancy passes and youth arrives; youth departs and manhood comes; then manhood decays and old age creeps upon us, as if without notice. In this way, Satan departs from lesser and weaker sins so that he may **re-enter** through greater and stronger ones. Indeed, he may even stop certain **great sins**; but even then, he still aims to bring in greater—even the greatest—wickedness, so that he may reign solely and absolutely, without any control or rebuke at all.

In the same way, the Devil goes about (as the Apostle *Peter*, or rather *Job*, says) and encompasses the earth, walking to and fro in it; and for the most part, he does this without making any noise or violent disturbance <note>original: "Renting" – a tearing or forceful disruption</note> at all.

<margin>Answer.</margin>
No, certainly not. But these words are so hard and difficult to reconcile that in the days of *Arius* <note>Arius (c. 250–336 AD) was a priest whose teachings that Christ was a created being subordinate to God the Father sparked the Arian controversy and led to the Nicene Creed.</note> it filled the church with *errors* and *heresies*. But so that I may answer *this doubt* and make it clear, I will lay down two principles.

First, although God receives *no new power* in himself, yet he does receive *power* by being made further known to man. And secondly, by man being made *further known to him*.

First, by his being made *further known* to *man*; the revealing and discovering of God to man, making himself *more known*—the manifestation of this is said *to add power* to him. However, this does not mean *that anything can be added to him who is infinite*; if there could, he would not be infinite, and *he would not be God*.

But know this: whatever attribute God has ascribed to him, it is in regard to *his creatures, not*...

Yet, I remember I was taught when I was a child—either by my *nurse*, or my *mother*, or my *schoolmaster*—that God Almighty was above in Heaven, namely above the *sun*, *moon*, and *stars*; and for a long time afterward, I thought that his court and his "presence chamber" <note>The room where a monarch formally receives guests.</note> were located there. But I assure you, I had more work to do to *unlearn this principle* than I ever had to *learn* it; and I am afraid too *many* of us have gone no further than this *childish principle*, which leads to many errors.

But it is safer to take *Heaven* in the broadest sense: either as God filling all places and *all things*, as well above the sun as below, and below as above; and so *Heaven* is *wherever God is*, which is everywhere. For he cannot be excluded from any place; but he is not only in every place, but he is in every place equally.

### *An illustration: two drops reasoning together.*

Suppose two drops of water, apart from the sea, should reason together, and one should say to the other:

"Where do we come from? Can you conceive where we are from—either where we originated, to whom we belong, or where we shall go? We are something, but what will become of us in a short time? Can you tell?" And the other drop answered:

"Alas, *poor fellow-drop*, be assured *we are nothing*; for the *sun may rise and draw us up, and scatter us, and so bring us to nothing*."

The other says again, "Suppose it does; for all that, we still exist; we have a being <note>original: "being," meaning existence or essential nature</note>; we are something."

Here follow several brief collections from
certain sublime and spiritually disciplined <note>original: "Mortified"; in this context, it refers to authors who have "died" to the world through self-denial and asceticism</note> authors,

### *What the Divine Mist or Darkness is.*

O TRINITY! You who are *beyond* ESSENCE <note>original: "ESSENCE" (Greek: *ousia*); referring to the fundamental nature or being of God. Dionysius argues God is "beyond being."</note>, beyond GOD, and beyond *goodness*, the Governor of *Christian wisdom* concerning God: Grant to *direct* us to the *more-than-unknown, more-than-shining, highest peak* of *mystical oracles* <note>meaning: the sacred revelations of God understood through spiritual intuition rather than logic</note>, where the *simple*, *absolute*, and *unchangeable* MYSTERIES of Divinity *are hidden*. They are hidden by the *more-than-radiant* MIST <note>original: "MISTINES"; this refers to the "Divine Dark," a state where God is so bright He seems dark to human senses</note> of *secret-teaching* SILENCE in the *darkest darkness*. This is He who *outshines* that which is *more-than-most-glorious*, and—underneath that which is *utterly intangible and invisible*—*more-than-fills* the blinded or *eyeless minds* <note>meaning: those who have set aside their physical and intellectual "sight" to perceive God directly</note> with *more-than-beautiful radiance*.

2. And *these things* I pray for; but as for you, my friend *Timothy*, through your *most intent study* and exercise...

This is because it admits neither speech nor understanding, for it is SUPER-ESSENTIAL <note>original: "Super-essential" (Greek: *hyperousios*); meaning existing beyond the very category of "being" or "essence"</note>, standing *super-eminent* above all things. Then he is separated from the *multitude* and, with the selected priests, he labors up to the top of the divine ascents. <margin>1.</margin>It is this that we pray for: that we may be in <margin>10</margin> this mist that shines far above the light. By *unseeing* and *unknowing*, we may *see* and *know* *that* which is *above* all sight and *knowledge*. Indeed, in *that state*, we do not *see* nor *know* at all. For *this* is *to see and know truly*, and *super-essentially* <note>original: "Super-Effentially"; a term describing God's existence as being "beyond" or "above" all created essence or being.</note> to praise *Him* who is *super-essential*. This is done by the *taking away* of all things *that exist*. It is just like those who would create a *hand-carved statue* <note>original: "Self-ingraven Image"; the author uses the metaphor of a sculptor who reveals a form not by adding material, but by chipping away the excess stone.</note>, taking away all the *obstructions* that stand before the pure *sight* of that which is *hidden*. Only by *taking away* do they show forth *that* which is *concealed* and *covered* by its own material.

And we must (as I think) praise and commend NEGATIONS <note>original: "TAKINGS-AWAY"; in Greek, *aphaeresis*. This refers to "apophatic theology," the practice of describing God by what He is not (e.g., God is not finite, not mortal).</note> in contrast to *positions* and *affirmations*. Regarding *affirmations*, we established them by beginning at the first principle and ascending through the middle steps to the last. But here, making our *ascent* from the <margin>11</margin> last back to the *Most-Ancient*, we take away all things so that we may know without any VEIL that Unknown one, who is all things that exist, or is

## CHAPTER III.

### *What Statements About God are Affirmative, and what are Negative.*

1. In our *Theological Descriptions* <note>This refers to a previous (and now lost) work by Dionysius titled *Theological Outlines* or *Theological Representations*.</note>, we have expressed the *most* fundamental aspects of *affirmative* divinity <note>original: "affirmative Divinity"; also known as cataphatic theology, which describes God through positive titles like "Good," "Wise," or "Life."</note>: how the *divine* and good *nature* is called *One*, and how it is *Three*; what it is within that nature which is called FATHERHOOD and SONSHIP <note>original: "PATERNITY & FILIAL"</note>; and *what* the divinity of the HOLY SPIRIT <note>original: "HOLY GHOST"</note> means. We described how from the *immaterial* and *indivisible* GOOD, there sprang out the *heart-felt* lights of goodness, which still remained within Him, never *leaving* (since the *dwelling-place* of being is CO-ETERNAL to its *outflowing* or *budding forth* <note>original: "Emanation or Germination"</note>)—remaining both in *Himself*, in *themselves*, and in *one another*.

2. We also described how the *super-essential JESUS* <note>original: "Super-essential JESUS"; a term used to describe Christ as existing "beyond essence" or "above being" as the Second Person of the Trinity.</note> took on a real existence <note>original: "essentiated"</note> in the truths of *human nature*: as well as *other things* which we have *celebrated* in our *Theological Descriptions*, as they were delivered to us from the *Scriptures*.

<summary>In this passage, Dionysius summarizes his previous work on "affirmative theology," detailing the nature of the Trinity and the Incarnation of Jesus, before contrasting these positive descriptions with the mystical "darkness" of negative theology.</summary>
<keywords>Dionysius the Areopagite, affirmative divinity, Trinity, Holy Spirit, Incarnation, super-essential, emanation, Theological Descriptions</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Chapter 3 of "The Mystical Theology," where Dionysius discusses his previous writings to illustrate how theology becomes more concise as it moves from physical symbols toward the absolute mystery of God.</meta>

<page-num>423</page-num>
<header>of Dionysius the Areopagite.</header>

3. In the same way, in the book *On Divine Names*, we explained how He is called GOOD, how He is BEING, how He is LIFE, WISDOM, and POWER, and whatever else belongs to the *intelligible* naming of God <note>original: "Intelligible Divine NOMINATION"; this refers to names for God that describe abstract concepts rather than physical things.</note>.

4. However, in our *Symbolical Theology* <note>original: "Symbolical Divinity"; this refers to a lost work by the author that explained physical metaphors for God found in Scripture.</note>, we showed what the metaphors <note>original: "Metonymies, or Translations or Borrowed NAMES"</note> are that are taken from physical <note>original: "sensible"</note> things and applied to the Divine. These include the Divine FORMS; the Divine *figures or shapes, parts, organs, or instruments*; the *Divine places and ornaments*; the *angers, sorrows, and furies*; the *drunkenness and overindulgence* <note>original: "Surfets"</note>; the *oaths and curses*; the *sleeping and waking*; and other similar things belonging to this part of theology <note>original: "Divinity"</note> called "Symbolical." In that work, we spoke of those *forms and figures* that have been sacredly <note>original: "Holily"</note> invented to represent God.

5. And I think you have noticed, just as I have, how many more words are used in that later work than in the earlier ones. It was necessary for the *Theological Outlines* <note>original: "Descriptions"</note> and the explanation of the *Divine Names* to use fewer words than *Symbolical Theology*. This is because the *higher* we climb toward that which is *above*, the more our words are narrowed <note>original: "Contracted"</note> and concentrated into the simple vision <note>original: "View and Sight"</note> of spiritual <note>original: "Intelligible"</note> things.

<margin>12</margin> Similarly, now that we are entering into that DARKNESS which is beyond all mind and understanding, we will find not just brevity of speech, but *utter silence* and *wordlessness* <note>original: "dumbness"</note>, as well as a lack of understanding <note>The author means that human reason fails when faced with the absolute mystery of God.</note>.

<summary>Dionysius explains that while symbolic theology uses many words to describe God through physical metaphors, mystical theology leads to total silence as the soul enters the divine darkness beyond all understanding.</summary>
<keywords>Dionysius the Areopagite, Divine Names, Symbolical Theology, divine darkness, apophatic theology, silence, spiritual ascent</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Chapter 3 of "The Mystical Theology," where Dionysius explains why the language of theology must shrink as it approaches the divine mystery. He contrasts the "descending" path of positive description (Affirmation) with the "ascending" path of stripping away those descriptions (Negation).</meta>

<page-num>424</page-num>
<header>The Mystical Divinity</header>

And from there, our *speech* and *discourse*—descending from the *Highest* to the *Lowest*—is *enlarged* into a proportional *breadth* or *multitude* according to the degree of its *descent*.

<margin>13</margin>
But now, *arising* from the things *below* to that which is *above*, our speech is *contracted* and grows *less* according to the measure of its *ascent*. After the entire ascent is finished, it becomes completely *void* of words and is thus united to that which is *unspeakable*.

6. But you will ask: to what purpose is this? Why, when laying down the *Divine Affirmations* <note>original: "Affirmations"; the "kataphatic" way of theology that describes God by what He is (e.g., God is Good).</note>, did we begin with the *first* and highest, yet now we begin the *Divine Negations* <note>original: "Ablations or takings away"; the "apophatic" way of theology that describes God by what He is NOT (e.g., God is not a stone).</note> with the *last* and lowest? 

I answer: when we were describing that which was *above all affirmation* <note>original: "Position"</note>, it was fitting to *begin* and *establish* the fundamental *affirmations* with those things that were *most proper* and *nearest* to Him. But now, when we move by way of *taking away* attributes from that which is *above all negation* <note>original: "Ablation"</note>, it is likewise fitting that we should begin our "takings away" with *those* things that are furthest removed from Him.

For is He not, *rather* and more properly, *Life* and *Goodness* than *air* or *a stone*? And may it not *rather* and more *properly* be said that He is not *weak* or *angry*, than that He is not *spoken* or *understood*?

<summary>Dionysius explains that as the soul ascends to God, language must simplify and eventually cease. He justifies starting negative theology by rejecting the lowliest physical descriptions first, as they are the furthest from God's true nature.</summary>

## CHAP. IV.

### *That He who is preeminently the Cause of all sensible things, is yet no sensible thing at all.*

1. We say, therefore, that the *Cause* of all things—which is *above all* things—is neither lacking in nor without *Essence* <note>original: "Essence"; the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing.</note>, nor *Life*, nor *Reason*, nor *Mind*.

2. Neither is it *a body*, nor does it have *shape*, *form*, *quality*, *quantity*, or *size*. It is not in any *place*, nor is it *seen*, nor can it be *sensed by touch*.

3. It neither *perceives* through the *senses*, nor can it be *perceived* by the *senses*. It has neither *disorder* nor *turmoil*, as if it were *disturbed* by material *passions* <note>original: "Passions"; in this context, the term refers to being acted upon or undergoing change, rather than just human emotions.</note>.

4. It is not *powerless*, as if it were subject to physical *passions* or *accidents* <note>original: "Accidents"; in classical philosophy, these are non-essential properties that can change without altering the core nature of an object.</note>. Neither is it in *any* need or *poverty* of light; it does not need any *light* to see *by* or *with*.

5. It possesses neither *alteration*, nor *corruption* <note>original: "Corruption"; the process of decaying or breaking down into parts.</note>, nor *division*, nor *deprivation*, nor *flux* (meaning a *continual flowing* and *succession of parts*), nor any other *sensible thing* <note>original: "Sensible thing"; anything that can be detected or understood through the five senses.</note>. Nor is it *any* of all these things.

<summary>In this chapter, Dionysius begins the "negative way" of theology by arguing that the Divine Cause is not a physical or material object. He lists various sensory qualities—such as size, location, and changeability—and asserts that God transcends all of them.</summary>

<keywords>Dionysius the Areopagite, Mystical Theology, apophatic theology, negation, transcendence, essence, sensible things, divine cause</keywords>

## Chap. V.

### *That He who is preeminently the Cause of all intelligible things, is none of those intelligible things.*

1. **AND** descending further, we say that the Cause is neither *Soul* nor *Mind*. It possesses neither *fantasy* <note>original: "Phantasie"; the mental faculty of creating or holding images.</note>, nor *imagination*, nor *opinion*, nor *reason*, nor *understanding*. Neither is it Reason or Understanding itself, nor can it be *spoken of* or *understood*.

2. It is neither *number*, nor *order*, nor *greatness*, nor *smallness*. It is neither *equality* nor *inequality*, nor *likeness* nor *unlikeness*.

<margin>14</margin>
3. It neither *stands still*, nor is it *moved*, nor does it *rest*. It neither has *power*, nor is it *power* or *light*. It neither *lives* nor is it *life*. It is neither *essence*, nor *eternity*, nor *time*, nor is there any *intellectual touch* <note>original: "Intellectual Touch"; a direct, non-sensory mental grasp or contact with a concept.</note> of it.

<margin>15</margin>
4. It is neither *knowledge*, nor *truth*, nor *kingship*, nor *wisdom*. It is neither *one thing*, nor *unity*, nor *godhead*, nor *goodness*.

<margin>16</margin>
5. Neither is it a *spirit*, as we can know or understand one, or according to *our* manner of *knowledge*. It is neither SONSHIP, nor FATHERHOOD, nor any other thing *known to us*, or to any *other* existing things.

6. Neither is it any of the things *that are not*, nor any of the things *that are*. Neither do the things *that are* know it *as it is*, nor does It know the *things that are* as they *are* <note>This suggests God's knowledge is not "subjective" or "objective" in the way human knowledge is; He does not learn about things from the outside.</note>.

<summary>This page concludes the treatise by arguing that God transcends all intellectual categories, including reason, power, and even the theological titles of "Father" and "Son." This "apophatic" approach suggests that the Divine is so far beyond human comprehension that it can only be described by what it is not.</summary>
<keywords>Pseudo-Dionysius, Mystical Theology, apophatic theology, negation, via negativa, divine nature, intellect, Fatherhood, Sonship</keywords>

# Dr. Everard’s ADVICE upon these following Sentences in Latin and English.

Do not read what follows until you have *read* and *felt*, and understand what goes before. For here follow certain *serious* and *notable* sayings, by which the diligent disciple of Christ may examine himself, and know what is to be thought or determined concerning the true and inward union to the *only* and *supreme* Good. This is so that we may depart from ourselves; and being dead to our own will, may live to God alone and to his will. Grant it, O God, through him who resigned his own will to his Heavenly Father, who lives and reigns with the Holy Spirit in a perfect Trinity forever. *Amen.*

Because of their concise and forceful shortness, these sayings would be hard to understand if put into as few words as the Latin. I have, therefore, not only translated them into English, but also attached the Latin to them, so that where one language is obscure, it may be helped by the other.

# The Sayings of a Certain

In conclusion, I will add <note>original: "Annex"</note> to this the judgment of *John Denck* <note>original: "Iohn Denqui"; likely referring to Hans Denck (c. 1495–1527), a radical German theologian</note> concerning the Holy Scriptures, which he made in his *Recantation* shortly before his death and which was later printed.

"I do," (he says) "prefer the *Holy Scriptures* above all *human treasure*. Yet, I do so in such a way that I do not value them as much as the *Word of God*, which is *living, powerful, and eternal*. This Word is *free* and at liberty from all the *elements* of this world. For if that Word is God himself, it follows that it is *Spirit*—not the literal text <note>original: "Letter"</note>—written without pen or ink, so that it can never be *erased* <note>original: "Obliterated"</note>. 

For this reason, *true happiness* <note>original: "felicity"</note>, or the Word of God, is not tied to the *letter* of the Scriptures. The reason is that it is impossible for an *evil* mind to be *reformed* <note>original: "Amended"</note> by the Scriptures alone, though it may be made more learned. But a *good* mind—that is, the kind that is endowed with any spark of *divine devotion* <note>original: "Divine study"</note> or knowledge—is made better by *all things*. 

Thus, the Holy Scriptures are *pure* <note>original: "Clean"</note> to those who are *pure, good, and wholesome* (that is, to those endowed with the *Holy Spirit*). But to the *unclean* and *unbelievers*, the Scriptures—like all other things—are *unclean and deadly*."

In this way, then, it is possible that a person chosen by God may be saved without *preaching*, or the

This concludes his point.

All these things aim at this: that we should, by a *received power* from God, do our best to hunger for God and His word. We should not proceed so confidently with only the *dead letter* <note>original: "Killing Letter"; a reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6, "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life"</note> of the *Scriptures*. Instead, while giving them all *fitting honor*, we should recognize them to be a certain *image, brilliance, lantern, scabbard, manger*, and *vestry* <note>original: "Vestry"; a room in a church where sacred garments are kept, suggesting the Scripture "clothes" the Word</note> of the Word. But we know that while these things are being said, there are some who are greatly *troubled* and *offended*. Just as in the case of the Virgin *Mary*, they say we would *reject* the Scriptures. To this we reply: there can never be *too much honor* given to them. But the truth is, when the *honor due to God alone* is attributed to the Scriptures—just as it is with *Mary*—it becomes the *worship of idols*. Out of the Scriptures, as with *Mary*, a certain *idol* is made, <margin>☞</margin> which is *placed, honored, valued, adored*, and *consulted* in the place of God.

The Scriptures indeed, as a holy thing, ought to inspire *awe* <note>original: "Terror"; here meaning profound religious reverence or holy dread</note> in men, and should be *read* with *religious fear and trembling*. And, as was said before, they are to be

<header>### ...and are not the Word of God</header>

[The Scriptures should] be preferred above all earthly treasure, but not made equal to God *and His Word*. The Scriptures (like the Law and all other things) *are good* for the good, who alone know *how* to use them well.

...in *unity*: He shall *close off* <note>original: "Shut up"; meaning to withdraw from external distractions.</note> all his *senses* in *quietness*, *continually praying* and *calling* upon *God*. *His* eye shall be *fixed* on God in all his actions. ### ->The P R A Y E R.<-

> *May the almighty power of God the Father vanquish and overcome in us whatever may hinder us from him, and give us strength to do his most acceptable will in all things. May the most bright wisdom of God enlighten us and lead us to all good things which may bring us forward to him alone. May the unspeakable and super-abounding love of the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note> pierce through all the opposition in us; may it kindle and unite our love unto himself with a most ardent and pleasant turning of all our powers and strengths. Thus, forgetting those things that are behind, we may follow his most sweet calling and loving drawing <note>original: "Amorous drawing"; the attractive power of divine love pulling the soul toward God.</note>—to which, from eternity, the more-than-most glorious Trinity has predestined us. This path leads from the love of this deceitful world to the enjoyment of himself and to all his riches and infinite blessedness, so that by grace we may be made what we are not, and cannot be by nature. To him be all praise, obedience, and reverence from every creature, throughout infinite ages. Amen.*

## Divine and a Beggar.

A certain *Divine* <note>original: "Divine"; a theologian or member of the clergy, specifically identified here as the 14th-century German mystic Johannes Tauler.</note>, who (if we may believe the ancient *manuscripts* <note>original: "Copies"</note>) was *John Tauler* himself, met with *a Beggar* and had this *discourse*, *containing a most excellent example of a perfect man;* from which we may be taught *how in all things we ought to be of the same mind, resigned to the will and appointment of God*.

There was in times past a certain famous *Divine*, who for the space of eight years had continually *importuned* <note>original: "importuned"; persistently pleaded with or urged.</note> the Lord by prayer, conceiving that he lacked <note>original: "wanted"</note> the *right knowledge of the Truth*, despite all his *learning*. He spent whole *nights* in this pursuit, begging of God to let him know *Him* and know *himself*, and to show him *any man* who might teach him *the way of Truth*. And when on one occasion he was *inflamed* with a most *vehement* <note>original: "Vehement"; intense or passionate.</note> desire for this, a voice from *Heaven* spoke to him in this way: *“Go forth to the church doors and there you shall find a man who can teach you the way of Truth.”* And going forth, he found there a certain BEGGAR with *patched* and *torn* apparel and filthy, dirty feet, whose whole *outfit* <note>original: "Apparel"</note> was scarcely worth three half-pence; to whom by

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the learned Divine (theologian) and the beggar. Having previously established that he is never unhappy because he accepts everything as God's will, the beggar now explains the depth of his spiritual resignation.</meta>

->A Learned Divine and a Beggar.<-

I am fully resolved, *through his grace*, to adhere and only to cling <note>original: "cleave"</note> to the will of God as the best (abandoning *my own will*). Into his will I have so wholly poured out *my own will* that whatever *He wills*, *I will* also. For this reason (as I said), I was never *unhappy*, seeing that I will *cling to his will alone* and have wholly resigned *my own personal will*.

*Divine.* This is very strange. But tell me, I pray you, what would you say if the Lord of Majesty were to *drown you* in the *bottomless pit*? Could you then be content with *His will*?

*Beggar.* Drown me in the *bottomless pit*? Why, certainly, if he should, I have *two arms* with which I would still embrace Him and clasp Him fast. One is *true humility*, which I lay beneath Him; and through *Him*, I am *united* to *His most sacred humanity*. The other is the *right arm*, which is *love*, which is united to his *divinity*. And *by* this love *given* to me from *Himself*, I hold him *so fast* that he would be *forced* to go down to *Hell* with me. And it would be *much more* desirable to me to be in *Hell with God* than to be in *Heaven without him*.

From this, the DIVINE learned that the most *direct* <note>original: "Compendious"; meaning the shortest or most efficient path</note> way to God is *true resignation* with profound *humility*. Thereupon the *Divine* spoke again to the *Beggar* and asked him:

*Divine.* Good Lord, where did you come from?
*Beggar.* From *God*.
*Divine.* Where did you find God?
*Beggar. Right there*, where I left all created things <note>original: "Creatures"; refers to all worldly things created by God, rather than the Creator himself</note>.

# The Chapters of the Individual Sermons Analyzed, which may serve as a Table of Contents.

### Part 1.

Upon this text, *Mark 9:50*: "Have salt in yourselves," he first stirs the audience to attention, and then:

He shows:
1. What salt is.
2. What it is to *have* salt.
3. What it means to have it in ourselves.
Page 3.

Several interpretations of what is meant by salt, page 6.
In what sense the *Apostles* were called salt, page 7.

Christ is the salt:
1. To season our duties; nothing from man is accepted, only Jesus Christ in us. p. 9.
2. To heal our sin-wounds, p. 11.
3. To preserve the soul from decay <note>original: "putrefaction"</note>, p. 13.
4. Salt has a power <term>virtue</term> to preserve itself.

All God's promises are as a *Covenant of salt* <note>original: "Covenant of salt"; an ancient biblical idiom for an unbreakable, eternal agreement, as salt was a preservative</note> like himself, unalterable: it is childishness to think God is altered or changed by prayer. p. 13, 14.

The fifth and main reason (as the author understands it): just as salt is the substance and binder <note>original: "knitter"</note> of all things, so Christ is the salt of the salt. p. 15, 16, 17.

*Objection:* Since Christ compares himself to salt: if Christ can lose his flavor <note>original: "favour"; meaning savor or saltiness</note> as salt does and be good for nothing, in what sense may this be said regarding Christ? This is answered under the two heads explained, p. 18, etc.

The Exhortation by way of Application <note>original: "Use"; a common term in 17th-century preaching for the practical application of a doctrine</note>, p. 29.

The third head is: to see that we have salt in ourselves, and to stop judging <note>original: "censuring"</note> and condemning others, p. 30, etc.

### Four Sermons on Joshua 15:15–16. *And Caleb said, "He who strikes Kiriath-sepher and takes it, to him I will give Achsah my daughter as a wife," etc.*
